changes.adapted_text: Given a nonzero smooth Navier–Stokes profile that repeats in logarithmic time up to an isometry and satisfies $|W(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-1}$, we construct finite-energy solutions of the unforced equations that blow up with this profile. On $\mathbb R^3$ we cut off a vector potential to obtain smooth, compactly supported solenoidal data, then adjust finitely many components of the datum to obtain the prescribed rate of approach. This requires no spectral stability assumption on the profile. The whole-space solution satisfies $\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^2}\asymp(1-t)^{-1/4}$. For smooth data on $\mathbb T^3$ the corresponding rate is $\|u_{\mathrm{per}}(t)\|_{H^1}\asymp(T-t)^{-1/4}$. In similarity variables the gradients converge to the profile gradient in $L^2$, on $\mathbb R^3$ and on expanding balls, respectively. A second theorem constructs the required exact profile when an approximate family satisfies quantitative certificate conditions. Alpöge and Buckmaster report checking these conditions for a particular family by interval arithmetic. With that input, the two theorems give breakdown of global smooth existence on both domains with zero force. The certificate data and verification calculation do not accompany this edition (Subsection 1.5).

changes.authors_text: We prove that there exist smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial data on $\mathbb R^3$, and smooth divergence-free initial data on the torus $\mathbb T^3$, for which the solutions of the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations without force blow up in finite time. This disproves the statements (A) and (B) of the Millennium Prize problem as formulated by Fefferman, and hence proves the statements (C) and (D). These solutions converge in self-similar variables to a backward discretely self-similar solution and blow up at its rate, which is $(T-t)^{-1/4}$ in $\dot H^1$. The discretely self-similar solution is obtained from a certificate: an approximate solution that satisfies explicit inequalities. The certificate will be released soon; its hash is `3f7a335b84b6c7631742cacc5343dfcd11cf72f5221ff79b2b9268790b4b22c5`.

changes.note: Distinguishes the orthogonal returns in the present theorem from the rotations in Bradshaw and Tsai, Open Problem 5.1.
changes.adapted_text: In Leray’s backward self-similar ansatz \[[70](#cite-ref70), §20, pp. 224–225\], $u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}U(x/\sqrt{T-t})$. At the shrinking spatial scale $\sqrt{T-t}$ a single velocity field $U$ describes every phase. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76), Theorem 1, p. 291\] exclude a nonzero such $U$ in $L^3$, and Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86), Theorems 1–2, p. 31\] excludes it in particular in $L^6$, the space allowed by our decay bound. Consider instead a field $W$ that evolves in logarithmic time $s$ and returns after a fixed interval $S$, so that $W(s+S,y)=W(s,y)$. In physical variables the same motion then takes place on successively smaller scales. <!-- source-page: 2 --> More generally the return may include an orthogonal change of coordinates. For returns by rotations, Bradshaw and Tsai ask whether every such backward solution with $|u(t,x)|\le C/(|x|+\sqrt{T-t})$ stays bounded up to $T$ \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.1, preprint p. 22\]. The bound allows a critical $|x|^{-1}$ tail, and finite rotational symmetry leaves room for angular dependence. Subsection 1.3 gives the corresponding $L^3$, axisymmetry and small-period exclusions.
changes.authors_text: Leray \[[70](#cite-ref70), §20\] proposed to look for singular solutions of (1.1) among the backward self-similar ones, $u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}\,U(x/\sqrt{T-t})$. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76)\] and Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86)\] proved that there is no such solution other than zero, under natural integrability conditions on the profile $U$. The next candidate is a solution that is invariant under the scaling of the equations for one scaling factor only, possibly after a rotation: a discretely self-similar <!-- source-page: 2 --> solution. Whether a nonzero solution of this kind exists backward in time, with the bound $|u(t,x)|\le C\,(|x|+\sqrt{T-t})^{-1}$, is the subject of \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.1\].

changes.adapted_text: Theorem 1.1 starts from a nonzero solution of this kind. On $\mathbb R^3$ a correction in a fixed finite-dimensional space of initial velocities suffices to follow the profile into the singularity. We obtain solutions from compactly supported data on $\mathbb R^3$ and from periodic data on $\mathbb T^3$ whose rescaled velocities approach the profile. The construction requires no spectral hypothesis on the profile. Theorem 7.1 constructs the profile used in this argument. A family of approximate profiles, together with data satisfying the certificate conditions, yields the required exact profile. Corollary 7.2 composes the two implications. Its consequence for Fefferman’s alternatives \[[53](#cite-ref53), (A)–(D), pp. 1–2\] is given in Subsection 2.3.
changes.authors_text: In this paper we prove that smooth solutions of (1.1) can blow up in finite time: there exist smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free data on $\mathbb R^3$, and smooth divergence-free data on $\mathbb T^3$, whose solutions are smooth up to a finite time, at which they blow up. In the formulation of the regularity problem by Fefferman \[[53](#cite-ref53)\], this disproves his statements (A) and (B) and hence proves his statements (C) and (D). The proof has two parts. The first is Theorem 1.1: one smooth discretely self-similar solution of the kind above implies this blow-up. Its proof shows that such a solution is stable in $\dot H^1$ up to finitely many directions, whatever the spectrum of its linearization is. The second is Theorem 7.1: such a solution exists near an approximate one that satisfies explicit inequalities, which we call a certificate.

changes.note: Iterates (1.2) in (1.4) at integer periods, allowing any orthogonal R. The identity exhibits physical time, length and velocity at a common phase of the exact reference field.
Derives the positive periodic leading term in the whole-space gradient norm, and integrates its squared blow-up rate in the physical energy balance.
changes.adapted_text:
*The blow-up rate.* The change of variables gives $\|
abla u_T^*(t)\|_{L^2}=(T-t)^{-1/4}\|
abla W(s)\|_{L^2}$. The function $s\mapsto\|
abla W(s)\|_{L^2}$ is continuous, positive and $S$-periodic (Lemma 4.2). In the whole space, (1.6) and the reverse triangle inequality therefore give $(1-t)^{1/4}\|
abla u(t)\|_2=\|
abla W(-\log(1-t))\|_2+O((1-t)^\kappa)$. The leading coefficient follows the phase of the orbit and may be constant. The power $-1/4$ is Leray’s lower-bound exponent \[[70](#cite-ref70), §21, p. 227\]. Its square is integrable at the singular time, since $\int_t^1(1-	au)^{-1/2}\,d	au=2\sqrt{1-t}$. Hence the divergence of the gradient norm is compatible with finite total viscous dissipation in the energy identity (Appendix A.2).
changes.authors_text:
The rate $(T-t)^{-1/4}$ is that of $u_T^*$: we have $\|
abla u_T^*(t)\|_{L^2}=(T-t)^{-1/4}\,\|
abla W(s,\cdot)\|_{L^2}$, and $\|
abla W(s,\cdot)\|_{L^2}$ is bounded above and below, uniformly in $s$ (Lemma 4.2). This is also the rate of the lower bound of Leray \[[70](#cite-ref70), §21\] for $\|
abla u(t)\|_{L^2}$ when a solution becomes singular at time $T$. In self-similar variables, $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}\,U(s,y)$, the second bound of (1.6) reads $\|
abla(U(s,\cdot)-W(s,\cdot))\|_{L^2}\le C\,e^{-\kappa s}$, so that $u$ converges to the profile. By (1.7) the same holds for $u_{\mathrm{per}}$ on the ball $B_{1/16}$, which in self-similar variables exhausts $\mathbb R^3$. The time $T$ and the radius $ rac1{16}$ come from the dilation of a torus of large period $L$ to $\mathbb T^3$, with $T=L^{-2}$ (Subsection 1.3).

Write $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}U(s,y)$ in the whole space. Then (1.6) gives $\|
abla_y(U(s)-W(s))\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}\le Ce^{-\kappa s}$. By (3.1) the velocities converge in $L^6$ at the same rate. In physical coordinates the upper bound on the gradient error can grow, but its ratio to $\|
abla u_1^*(t)\|_2$ is $O((1-t)^\kappa)$. On the torus set $\delta=T-t$ and $U_{\mathrm{per}}(s,y)=\sqrt\delta\,u_{\mathrm{per}}(t,\sqrt\delta\,y)$ using the periodic lift. Multiplication of (1.7) by $\delta^{1/4}$ bounds $\|
abla_y(U_{\mathrm{per}}(s)-W(s))\|_{L^2(B_{1/(16\sqrt\delta)})}$ by $C\delta^\kappa$. The ball expands in $y$ because its physical radius stays equal to $1/16$.

changes.note: Writes the finite-codimension statement with the fixed correction space preceding the choice of nearby compactly supported solenoidal datum.
changes.adapted_text: *Choice of initial data.* There exist $\varepsilon_0>0$ and a fixed finite-dimensional space $E$ of smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free fields with the following property. Given any divergence-free $w_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|\nabla(w_0-W(0,\cdot))\|_{L^2}\le\varepsilon_0$, one can choose $\gamma\in E$ so that the datum $w_0+\gamma$ gives a smooth finite-energy solution on $[0,1)$ satisfying (1.6) (Proposition 2.1 and Lemma 2.3). The datum $u_0$ in the theorem is one such sum. This choice of $\gamma$ for each nearby $w_0$ is the sense of stability in finite codimension used here.
changes.authors_text: These properties are not special to the datum $u_0$ that we construct. There exist $\varepsilon_0>0$ and a finite-dimensional space $E$ of smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free fields such that every divergence-free $w_0\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|\nabla(w_0-W(0,\cdot))\|_{L^2}\le\varepsilon_0$ becomes, after the addition of an element of $E$, the datum of a smooth solution of finite energy on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ which satisfies (1.6) (Proposition 2.1 and Lemma 2.3); the datum $u_0$ is of this form. In this sense the blow-up is stable in finite codimension.

changes.note: States the certificate hypotheses and the exact profile-to-solution implication. The numerical record now accompanies its digest in Subsection 1.5.
changes.adapted_text: To obtain the profile assumed in Theorem 1.1, we start with a family of approximate profiles, each with its own period. A certificate (Subsection 7.3) specifies the family, auxiliary fields and constants, and bounds on them. Among its hypotheses are estimates for every admissible perturbation of each family member. Theorem 7.1 selects one parameter and corrects the corresponding member to an exact profile with its period and prescribed symmetries. This profile satisfies (1.2) with $R=I$. Theorem 1.1 then gives both blow-up solutions (Corollary 7.2). Appendix B reduces the perturbation estimates to conditions on finitely many represented fields and numbers. <!-- source-page: 4 --> Figure 1 shows the computed field $\bar W$ from which the approximate profiles are formed. Its vorticity concentrates in an axial column and in two layers, one on either side of $y_3=0$, each opening into nineteen spiral arms. Appendix C describes how continuation and Newton iteration on an adaptive discretization produce $\bar W$ in floating-point arithmetic. The authors continued several azimuthal wave numbers before selecting nineteen. Two families of harmonics turn about the column in opposite senses. Rotation by $\pi$ about the $y_1$ axis exchanges them. To see why both rotations enter the proof, label the time and angle harmonics by $\iota=(\iota_1,\iota_2)\in\mathbb Z^2$ as in (B.2). At the computed period $\bar S$ the frequencies in the two rotating frames are $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$ and $4\pi(\iota_2-\iota_1)/\bar S$. A mode slow in both frames must satisfy $|\iota_2|\le j_*$ and $|\iota_2-\iota_1|\le j_*$ if the frequency cutoff is $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. Their intersection contains only finitely many lattice points, each still carrying a function of radius and height. Elsewhere a large frequency supplies a positive term in the multiplier estimate. Appendix B.2 bounds the transport and coupling errors against these gains at the actual periods $S(\alpha)$.
changes.authors_text: Theorem 1.1 assumes a profile. In Section 7 we obtain one from a certificate. A certificate, defined in Subsection 7.3, consists of a family of approximate profiles with their periods, and of further fields and numbers. The approximate profiles are approximate solutions of the first two equations of (1.2), periodic in $s$, and depend on finitely many parameters. The conditions of a certificate are of two kinds. Some are estimates that are to hold for every perturbation of the approximate profiles, among them an a priori estimate for the linearized equation. The others are explicit inequalities between norms of these fields and between these numbers, of the kind that a computation with rigorous bounds for its errors can verify. We prove that a certificate gives a profile whose isometry is the identity, close to one of the approximate profiles, with its period and with the symmetries that the certificate prescribes for these profiles (Theorem 7.1), and hence, by Theorem 1.1, blow-up from smooth, compactly supported data on $\mathbb R^3$ and from <!-- source-page: 4 -->

The certificate from which we obtain the profile is not printed in this paper: it will be released soon, and its hash is `3f7a335b84b6c7631742cacc5343dfcd11cf72f5221ff79b2b9268790b4b22c5`. It consists of data of the form described in Appendix B.1 that satisfy the conditions of Appendix B. changes.note: Brings the radial phase into physical variables at fixed nonzero position, as in the far-field representation in Appendix C.
changes.adapted_text: The arms also explain a choice of coordinates at large radius. The oscillatory factors used for $\bar W$ in Appendix C.1 have a radial phase asymptotic to a multiple of $2\log|y|$ plus a constant. The time phase combines with it through $2\log|y|-s=2\log|x|-\log T$ for $x\ne0$, by (1.4). Thus this leading oscillation has fixed phase at a fixed physical point as $t$ approaches $T$.
changes.authors_text: The approximate profiles of this certificate are formed from one field and from further fields computed from it. This field was found by a numerical computation in floating-point arithmetic: Newton’s method on an adaptive discretization, started from a state that was reached by continuation; we describe the computation in Appendix C. Figure 1 shows this field, which we denote by $\bar W$. It is not axisymmetric. It is invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/19$ about the $y_3$ axis and under the rotation by $\pi$ about the $y_1$ axis; it is periodic in $s$, with the computed period $\bar S\approx0.36$; and an advance of $s$ by $\bar S/2$ rotates it by the angle $\pi/19$ about the $y_3$ axis. The norm of its gradient in $L^2$ is of order $10^4$ at every time. The certificate prescribes these symmetries, so that the profile $W$ that Theorem 7.1 gives for it has them as well (Remark 7.3): it is a profile with the isometry $I$ and a period $S$, and also with the rotation by $\pi/19$ about the $y_3$ axis and the period $S/2$. In the terminology recalled above, its field $u_T^*$ is thus both a backward discretely self-similar and a backward rotated discretely self-similar solution. By (7.38) and the conditions of Appendix B it differs from one of the approximate profiles of the certificate by less than $0.017$ in $\dot H^1$ at every time.

changes.note: Places the construction before the extended historical comparisons and explains the choice of the homogeneous gradient norm from the velocity and gradient tails.
changes.adapted_text: The field $u^*=u_1^*$ associated with a profile is an exact solution on $[0,1)$. Its datum need not have finite energy. The decay in (1.3) places $W(s)$ in $L^6$ and its gradient in $L^2$ uniformly in $s$. After radial integration the tails of $|W|^6$ and $|\nabla W|^2$ are bounded by multiples of $r^{-4}\,dr$ and $r^{-2}\,dr$, whereas the bound for $|W|^2$ gives only a constant times $dr$. We therefore perturb $u^*$ in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, realized by divergence-free $L^6$ fields with square-integrable gradient. Proposition 4.1 gives the integral equation in this space. Once a solution has compactly supported smooth data, local $H^1$ theory and the energy inequality give smoothness and finite energy (Lemma 2.3). On the torus the corresponding space consists of periodic fields of mean zero.
changes.authors_text: The field (1.4) of a profile is a smooth solution of (1.1), and we construct the solutions of Theorem 1.1 as perturbations of it. We find the perturbation by a contraction argument for the integral formulation of (1.1), which the field $u_1^*$ satisfies on $[0,1)$ (Proposition 4.1). We work in the space $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ of the divergence-free fields in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$ with square integrable gradient, with the norm $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}=\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$: by (1.3) the gradient of $W(s,\cdot)$ is square integrable, uniformly in $s$, whereas $W(s,\cdot)$ itself need not be. On the torus we use the corresponding space of periodic fields of mean zero (Subsections 2.1 and 3.6). By the classical local theory of the equations in $H^1$, a solution of the integral formulation in one of these spaces whose datum is smooth and compactly supported, or smooth on the torus, is a smooth solution (Lemma 2.3).

changes.note: Identifies the contributions of one velocity gradient and the three-dimensional volume element to the physical tracking estimate.
changes.adapted_text: Write $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}U(s,y)$ and $v=u-u^*$. We seek $U(s)$ whose distance from $W(s)$ in $\dot H^1$ decays like $e^{-\kappa s}$. In $\|\nabla v(t)\|_2$, velocity and one derivative contribute $(1-t)^{-1}$ together, and the square root of the volume element contributes $(1-t)^{3/4}$. Together these factors give the power $-1/4$. Decay of the rescaled error by $e^{-\kappa s}=(1-t)^\kappa$ gives the physical gradient error $O((1-t)^{\kappa-1/4})$.

changes.note: Displays the tail formula and the explicit bound, identifies the homogeneous difference for every other initial value, and connects the linear sum to the nonlinear contraction.
changes.adapted_text:
Sample a scalar mode once per period. Suppose $x_{n+1}=a x_n+f_n$, $|f_n|\le C\Theta^n$ and $0<\Theta<\min(1,|a|)$. Summing backwards gives $$
 x_0=-\sum_{j\ge0}a^{-j-1}f_j,\qquad
 x_n=-\sum_{j\ge n}a^{n-j-1}f_j,\qquad
 |x_n|\le\frac{C\Theta^n}{|a|-\Theta}.
$$ Any other initial value leaves a nonzero multiple of $a^n$. Even when $|a|<1$, this part decays too slowly. In the nonlinear equation the contraction determines the inhomogeneous term and the trajectory together.

changes.note: Locates the contraction factor in the dilation, the essential spectral radius in a compact perturbation, and the finite-dimensional part beyond a selected spectral circle.
changes.adapted_text: To see which perturbations can have this decay, evolve the linearized equation about $W$ through one similarity period and undo the isometry $R$. This gives the monodromy operator $\mathcal M$ on $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$. For the free equation the evolution from $0$ to $s>0$ consists of heat flow for time $1-e^{-s}$ followed by the dilation $f\mapsto\sqrt\mu\,f(\sqrt\mu\,\cdot)$ with $\mu=e^{-s}$. Heat flow is contractive, and this dilation multiplies the gradient norm by $\mu^{1/4}$. Thus the free period map has norm at most $e^{-S/4}$. Its difference from $\mathcal M$ is compact. At positive heat times the localized operators in the integral equation are compact (Lemma 3.2), and (3.7) controls the integrable singularity at the endpoint (Lemma 4.4). Outside the disk of radius $e^{-S/4}$ the spectrum therefore consists of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity. Choose $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ with no spectrum on its circle. Only finitely many eigenvalues lie outside that circle (Lemma 4.5). <!-- source-page: 8 --> Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65), Lemma 2.7, preprint pp. 10–11\] use a compact perturbation of the free evolution for a forward self-similar background. The periodic forward construction of \[[17](#cite-ref17), §19, p. 74\] gives the same bound on the essential spectral radius.
changes.authors_text: The norm of $\dot H^1$ is subcritical: the scaling $f\mapsto\sqrt\mu\,f(\sqrt\mu\,\cdot)$ of the equations multiplies it by $\mu^{1/4}$. In self-similar variables the linear flow without the terms that come from $W$ is the heat flow up to time $1-e^{-s}$ followed by this scaling with $\mu=e^{-s}$, and therefore its norm on $\dot H^1$ is at most $e^{-s/4}$. The flow linearized about $W$ over one period, followed by the action of $R^{-1}$ on fields, is the monodromy operator $\mathcal M$. It differs from the corresponding free flow by a compact operator. Hence its essential spectral radius is at most $e^{-S/4}<1$, and for a suitable $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ outside the disc of radius $\Theta$ consists of finitely many eigenvalues of finite multiplicity. For a self-similar solution forward in time this is the <!-- source-page: 8 --> argument of Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65), Lemma 2.7\]; for a solution that is periodic in self-similar time it is used in \[[17](#cite-ref17), Section 19\], with the same bound for the essential spectral radius.

changes.note: Explains the initial correction in the spectral splitting. Moves the endpoint limitation to (4.18).
changes.adapted_text:
Set $\Theta=e^{-\kappa S}$, so $0<\kappa<1/4$. An eigenvalue of modulus strictly between $\Theta$ and $1$ gives decay, but slower than the required $\Theta^n$ after $n$ periods. We impose no requirement on whether any eigenvalue grows. For a perturbation to decay at the chosen rate its physical-variable norm must satisfy $$
\sup_{0\le t<1}\,(1-t)^{\frac14-\kappa}\,\|v(t)\|_{\dot H^1}<\infty,
$$ On the spectral subspace inside the circle, forward summation of the inhomogeneous terms over past periods gives the required decay. On the finite-dimensional exterior subspace, decay fixes the initial component through a sum over all future periods. The inverse powers in (4.11) play the role of $a^{-1}$ in the scalar example, and the power bounds there give convergence of both sums. To realize the prescribed component by a compactly supported correction, we choose smooth solenoidal fields whose projections form a basis of the exterior subspace. Their span is $E$ (Subsection 4.4). Its dimension and the chosen $\kappa$ depend on the profile and the spectral circle. The resulting right inverse (4.8) and a nonlinear contraction give, for each $w_0$ near $u^*(0)=W(0)$ in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}$, an element $\gamma\in E$ and a solution with datum $w_0+\gamma$ satisfying the displayed bound for $v$. The center, blow-up time and phase of the profile stay fixed.
changes.authors_text:
We assume nothing about these eigenvalues. In the program of \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] for non-uniqueness an unstable eigenvalue is the hypothesis, and in \[[17](#cite-ref17)\] the main difficulty is to construct a solution that has one. For blow-up it suffices that the eigenvalues outside the disc are finitely many: each of them, whatever its modulus, is removed by a correction of the datum in a finite-dimensional space. More precisely, let $\kappa\in(0,\tfrac14)$ be defined by $\Theta=e^{-\kappa S}$. We solve the equation linearized about $u^*$ in the space of the perturbations $v$ with $$
\sup_{0\le t<1}\,(1-t)^{\frac14-\kappa}\,\|v(t)\|_{\dot H^1}<\infty,
$$ which are those of size $e^{-\kappa s}$ in self-similar variables, and we leave the datum of $v$ free in a finite-dimensional space $E$, a complement of the invariant subspace of $\mathcal M$ on which its powers decay faster than $\Theta^n$. A Lyapunov–Perron argument over the periods of $u^*$ gives a bounded right inverse of this linear problem (Section 4). Since the smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free fields are dense in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, we can choose $E$ among them, and we need not know the regularity or the decay of the eigenfunctions of $\mathcal M$. A contraction then gives, for every $w_0$ in a ball of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ about $u^*(0)=W(0,\cdot)$, an element $\gamma$ of $E$ and a solution $u$ on $[0,1)$ with datum $w_0+\gamma$ such that $u-u^*$ lies in this space. We modulate neither the blow-up time, nor the location of the blow-up, nor the phase of $u^*$ in its period.

changes.adapted_text: For $w_0$ we take the field $u^*(0)$, cut off far from the origin. The cutoff is applied to a vector potential, so that the field remains divergence-free: for $0\le t<1$ and a radius $r>0$ we let $\bar u(t)=\operatorname{curl}\bigl(\eta(\cdot/r)\,A(t)\bigr)$, where $A(t)$ is the vector potential of $u^*(t)$ given in (5.1) and $\eta$ is a smooth cutoff that equals $1$ on $B_{1/2}$ and vanishes outside $B_1$. The field $\bar u(t)$ equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{r/2}$ and vanishes outside $B_r$, and by (1.3) its distance from $u^*(t)$ in $\dot H^1$ is at most a constant multiple of $r^{-1/2}$, uniformly in $t$ (Lemma 5.1). On $\mathbb R^3$ choose $r$ so that $Cr^{-1/2}\le\varepsilon_0$, the permitted distance from $W(0)$ in Proposition 2.1, and take $w_0=\bar u(0)$ (Subsection 5.2). In \[[17](#cite-ref17), §19, p. 75\] the datum is truncated in the same way, through the same potential. changes.note: Explains how localized interactions transfer the whole-space inverse to the torus; points to the kernel estimates in Section 6.
changes.adapted_text: On $\mathbb T^3$ it is the entire reference field that has to be localized. We first work at blow-up time one on $\mathbb T_L^3=\mathbb R^3/L\mathbb Z^3$, with $L$ large. At each time cut off the potential of $u^*$ at radius $L/8$, take its curl $\bar u(t)$ and periodize it. The resulting field $u^{\mathrm a}$ equals $u^*$ on $B_{L/16}$. To bound the interaction with translated copies, Lemma 6.1 uses the $|x|^{-4}$ decay of the kernel of the projected heat flow on divergences. The resulting residual has order $L^{-1/2}$ in the weighted gradient norm (Subsection 6.2). <!-- source-page: 9 --> In the periodic linearization, the terms containing $u^{\mathrm a}$ need the perturbation only on $B_{L/8}$, the support ball of the cutoff. Apply the whole-space inverse (4.8) to this localized interaction. Its correction supplies initial data for periodic heat flow, which reconstructs the perturbation on $\mathbb T_L^3$. This gives an approximate right inverse with operator error $O(L^{-1/2})$ (Lemma 6.3). Increasing $L$ makes the norm of this error less than one, so the Neumann series gives an exact right inverse. The nonlinear contraction now removes the residual of $u^{\mathrm a}$. Finally $u_{\mathrm{per}}(t,x)=L\,u(L^2t,Lx)$ takes the solution on $\mathbb T_L^3$ to the unit torus, with blow-up time $T=L^{-2}$.

changes.note: Uses a rank-one linear map to distinguish the force column from the constraint, explains translation of the time origin, and gives the order in which the nonlinear identity, adjoint bounds and projection produce zero total force.
changes.adapted_text:
The correction in Sections 4–6 changes the initial velocity. In Section 7 the unknown is the periodic orbit itself, including its period $S$. We set $\theta=s/S$ and give all trial orbits period one in $\theta$. A translate of an exact orbit is again an orbit, so differentiation with respect to the shift gives a null direction of the linearized equation. A phase condition fixes the time origin. To see the roles of the other constraints and forces, consider the linear map $L(x,y)=(x,0)$. The augmented equations $L(x,y)+(0,\beta)=(f_1,f_2)$ and $y=c$ determine $x=f_1$, $y=c$ and $\beta=f_2$. The constraint fixes the free coordinate, and the auxiliary force measures the mismatch in the second equation. If the data depend on a parameter, the original equation holds where that mismatch vanishes.

We add finitely many force coefficients and impose the same number of linear constraints. They can also be used for directions in which the linearized equation has a large response to small data. The certificate bounds the augmented inverse. Proposition 7.8 proves surjectivity by the Fredholm alternative. For a trial parameter $\alpha$ and a trial nonlinear term $g$, solve the augmented linear problem for a perturbation $v$ and force coefficients $\beta$. Proposition 7.10 updates $g$ to $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ and updates $\alpha$ by subtracting an invertible matrix times the total force $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta$, then projecting onto the parameter set. At a joint fixed point the equation is nonlinear because $g=(v\cdot\nabla)v$. Its adjoint estimates now put the *unprojected* update inside the set. The update must therefore equal $\alpha$, so the total force vanishes. Proposition 7.11 gives smoothness. The resulting unrotated recurrent velocity is continuous in time into $L^6$ by (3.1) and continuity of dilation, so the theorem of Chae and Wolf \[[26](#cite-ref26), Theorem 1.1, preprint p. 2\] gives the decay required in (1.3), with the derivative bound from Remark 1.2.

changes.note: Orders the stationary, scaling and rotation exclusions by the hypothesis that decides applicability, including dependence on the Type I constant. Names the comparison at the start of the paragraph.
changes.adapted_text:
*Restrictions on recurrent profiles.* A stationary solution of the similarity equation would give a self-similar solution in Leray’s sense. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76), Theorem 1, p. 291\] exclude nonzero stationary profiles in $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$. Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86), Theorems 1–2, p. 31\] excludes them in $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$ for $3<p<\infty$, and under local energy estimates. By (1.3) every slice of $W$ lies in $L^6$. Tsai’s result with $p=6$ therefore forces any nonzero profile considered here to depend on $s$. Bradshaw and Tsai \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.1, preprint p. 22\] ask whether every backward discretely self-similar solution with the Type I bound, possibly up to rotation, stays bounded through $T$. Under (1.5), any nonzero value gives velocities of magnitude $\lambda^{-n/2}|u_T^*(t,x)|$ at a sequence of points approaching $(T,0)$. Thus boundedness through $T$ would force the field to vanish.

For unrotated discrete self-similarity ($R=I$), Chae and Wolf \[[26](#cite-ref26), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3, preprint pp. 2–3\] prove that a smooth backward solution continuous into $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$, $3\le p<\infty$, satisfies the Type I bound. Conversely, given the bound with constant $C_W$, they exclude nonzero solutions whose expanding spatial scale $e^{S/2}$ is sufficiently close to one. Pineau and Vicol \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorems 1.6–1.7, pp. 6–7\] give a quantitative exclusion. For sufficiently small $S$ it also holds for rotations through angles $|\varphi|\le c S$, with both thresholds depending on $C_W$. The computed period alone therefore cannot decide applicability. A profile rotating continuously at a constant angular speed in $s$ would obey a rotated recurrence for every period. Bradshaw and Tsai record the question for such profiles as a problem of Perelman \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.2, preprint p. 22\]. For such steadily rotating profiles, \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorem 1.4, p. 4\] excludes angular speeds of sufficiently small or sufficiently large magnitude at a fixed Type I bound. Forward self-similar and discretely self-similar solutions do exist \[[64](#cite-ref64), [87](#cite-ref87), [12](#cite-ref12), [27](#cite-ref27)\], including solutions with rotation \[[13](#cite-ref13)\].
changes.authors_text:
The self-similar solutions of Leray are the solutions of the first two equations of (1.2) that do not depend on $s$. Nečas, Růžička and Šverák \[[76](#cite-ref76)\] proved that the only such solution with $W\in L^3(\mathbb R^3)$ is zero, and Tsai \[[86](#cite-ref86), Theorems 1 and 2\] proved the same for $W\in L^p(\mathbb R^3)$, $3<p<\infty$, and for the self-similar solutions that satisfy local energy estimates. In particular a profile depends on $s$, since its slices lie in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$. For discretely self-similar solutions, Open Problem 5.1 of \[[13](#cite-ref13)\] asks whether a backward solution with the Type I bound, rotated or not, remains bounded up to time $T$; by its self-similarity, a solution that remains bounded is zero, and by Remark 1.2 a smooth solution that is not zero is the field (1.4) of a profile. When $R=I$, Chae and Wolf \[[26](#cite-ref26), Theorems 1.1 and 1.3\] proved that the Type I bound holds for every smooth backward discretely self-similar solution that is continuous in time with values in $L^p(\mathbb R^3)$ for some $p\in[3,\infty)$, and that a smooth solution with this bound is zero if its scaling factor $e^{S/2}$ is close enough to $1$: the period $S$ of a profile with $R=I$ is bounded below by a positive number that depends only on $C_W$. Pineau and Vicol \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorems 1.6 and 1.7\] gave a quantitative proof and extended the statement to rotations $R$ by an angle at most $cS$, for a constant $c>0$ that depends only on $C_W$. Nonzero solutions with the Type I bound that are self-similar up to a rotation at a constant angular speed in $s$ would give profiles for every period; the question of their existence goes back to Perelman, as recorded by Bradshaw and Tsai \[[13](#cite-ref13), Open Problem 5.2\], and they are excluded for small and for large angular speeds \[[79](#cite-ref79), Theorem 1.4\]. Forward in time, self-similar and discretely self-similar solutions do exist \[[64](#cite-ref64), [87](#cite-ref87), [12](#cite-ref12), [27](#cite-ref27)\], also up to a rotation \[[13](#cite-ref13)\].

We write $u^*=u_1^*$. In the self-similar variables with blow-up time $1$, in which $u(t,x)=(1-t)^{-1/2}\,U(s,y)$, the equations (1.1) are the first two equations of (1.2) for $U$ and a pressure. The profile $W$ is a solution of these that is periodic up to $R$, and we look for solutions $U$ with $U(s)-W(s)\to0$ as $s\to\infty$.

changes.note: Distinguishes the critical tail envelope from the Barker–Prange two-sided logarithmic estimate for the cubic integral of a nonzero unrotated profile.
changes.adapted_text:
The spatial bound in (1.3) puts $u_T^*(t)$ in weak $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$ uniformly in $t$. The envelope $|y|^{-1}$ alone gives only $\int_1^r\rho^{-1}\,d\rho$ as an upper bound up to a constant for the tail of the cubic integral. When $R=I$, Barker and Prange \[[98](#cite-ref98), Corollary 1.1, p. 720\] show how strong $L^3$ fails. Translate the singular time to zero and apply their result with $p=6$. Smoothness and (1.3) give continuity into $L^6$ by dominated convergence on compact time intervals. At physical radius $r\sqrt{T-t}$ the cubic velocity integral equals $\int_{|y|<r}|W(s,y)|^3\,dy$. Their two bounds give growth comparable to $\log r$ for all sufficiently large $r$, uniformly in $s$. Thus no slice belongs to $L^3$. For Leray–Hopf solutions, Escauriaza, Seregin and Šverák \[[52](#cite-ref52), Theorem 1.3, preprint p. 5\] exclude singularities under a uniform-in-time bound in strong spatial $L^3$.

Several criteria exclude axisymmetric Type I singularities \[[28](#cite-ref28), [29](#cite-ref29), [69](#cite-ref69), [81](#cite-ref81)\]. In particular, (1.3) bounds $u_T^*$ both by $C_W/\sqrt{T-t}$ and by $C_W/r$ for cylindrical distance $r>0$ from the axis. An axisymmetric $u_T^*$ would remain bounded through $T$ by Koch, Nadirashvili, Seregin and Šverák \[[69](#cite-ref69), Theorem 6.2, preprint p. 21\], and (1.5) would then force it to vanish. The finite rotation group prescribed for the certificate is compatible with this exclusion. Albritton and Barker \[[1](#cite-ref1), Theorem 1.1 and (1.5), preprint p. 2\] characterize the existence of a suitable weak solution with a Type I singular point by the existence of a nontrivial mild bounded ancient solution satisfying their bounds on rescaled energy, dissipation, velocity and pressure. They also show that a nontrivial mild ancient solution uniformly bounded in weak $L^3$ along times tending to $-\infty$ yields a singular weak Leray–Hopf solution with forcing \[[1](#cite-ref1), (4.2) and Remark 4.3, preprint pp. 10, 12\]. The unforced solutions here come from localizing a recurrent profile.
changes.authors_text: By the first bound of (1.3), $u_T^*(t)$ is bounded in weak $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$, uniformly in $t$, and this gives no bound in $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$; for solutions that are bounded in $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$, singularities are excluded by the theorem of Escauriaza, Seregin and Šverák \[[52](#cite-ref52)\]. Singularities of Type I are excluded for axisymmetric solutions \[[28](#cite-ref28), [29](#cite-ref29), [69](#cite-ref69), [81](#cite-ref81)\]. Albritton and Barker \[[1](#cite-ref1)\] proved that a suitable weak solution with a Type I singular point exists if and only if there is a nontrivial mild bounded ancient solution, in the sense of \[[69](#cite-ref69)\], with Type I decay. By \[[1](#cite-ref1), Remark 4.3\], a nontrivial mild ancient solution that is bounded in weak $L^3(\mathbb R^3)$ along a sequence of times, as the field of a profile is, gives a singular weak Leray–Hopf solution of the equations with a force. Theorem 1.1 assumes a discretely self-similar solution and concludes blow-up without force, from smooth, compactly supported data on $\mathbb R^3$ and from smooth data on the torus.

changes.note: Groups precedents for the choice of initial data by equation, symmetry class and the number or type of exceptional directions. Names the comparison at the start of the paragraph.
changes.adapted_text:
*Localization and selection of initial data.* The choice of initial data has precedents in compressible flow. Merle, Raphaël, Rodnianski and Szeftel \[[74](#cite-ref74), [75](#cite-ref75)\] constructed self-similar Euler profiles and smooth spherical data whose Euler and Navier–Stokes solutions implode near them. For three-dimensional isentropic Euler, Buckmaster, Cao-Labora and Gómez-Serrano \[[16](#cite-ref16)\] obtained smooth imploding profiles for all adiabatic exponents larger than one. At exponent $7/5$ they proved Navier–Stokes implosion for a finite-codimensional set of smooth radial data with density bounded away from zero and constant at infinity. Cao-Labora, Gómez-Serrano, Shi and Staffilani \[[24](#cite-ref24)\] removed the symmetry assumption for both systems on $\mathbb R^3$ and on the torus. <!-- source-page: 6 --> For two-dimensional compressible Euler, Chen, Cialdea, Shkoller and Vicol \[[31](#cite-ref31)\] obtained vorticity blow-up by an axisymmetric implosion, with finitely many conditions on radial data and an open set of swirl velocities. See \[[30](#cite-ref30)\] for dimensions $d\ge3$ and \[[36](#cite-ref36)\] for non-isentropic implosions whose ground state is stable up to finitely many conditions without symmetry. Buckmaster and Iyer \[[19](#cite-ref19)\] obtained two-dimensional compressible Euler shocks that approach an unstable Burgers profile, with stability modulo two directions.

The number of data to adjust depends on the linearized dynamics. For incompressible Euler on $\mathbb R^3$, the $C^{1,\alpha}$ self-similar blow-up of Elgindi \[[47](#cite-ref47)\] gives finite-energy blow-up after one condition on axisymmetric perturbations \[[48](#cite-ref48), Theorem 2\]. For the one-dimensional nonlinear heat equation, Bricmont and Kupiainen \[[15](#cite-ref15), Theorems 1–2\] choose a parameter for each unstable direction of the renormalization map. Collot, Raphaël and Szeftel \[[38](#cite-ref38), Theorem 1.2\] obtain a finite-codimensional Lipschitz manifold of nonsymmetric data near a cutoff profile for the energy-supercritical heat equation, up to scaling and translation. For complex-valued Navier–Stokes solutions, Li and Sinai \[[71](#cite-ref71)\] produce blow-up by choosing parameters in ten-parameter families.
changes.authors_text:
For other equations, blow-up near a self-similar profile has been proved for sets of data of finite codimension: the linearization about the profile in self-similar variables has finitely many unstable directions, which are controlled through the choice of the data. Merle, Raphaël, Rodnianski and Szeftel \[[75](#cite-ref75)\] proved in this way the implosion of solutions of the compressible Euler and Navier–Stokes equations from smooth spherically symmetric data, near the smooth self-similar profiles of the Euler equations that they constructed in \[[74](#cite-ref74)\]. Buckmaster, Cao-Labora and Gómez-Serrano \[[16](#cite-ref16)\] constructed smooth self-similar imploding solutions of the isentropic compressible Euler equations in three dimensions for every adiabatic exponent larger than $1$ and proved, for the exponent $7/5$, the implosion of solutions of the compressible Navier–Stokes equations for a set of finite codimension of smooth radially symmetric data whose density is bounded away from zero and constant at infinity. Cao-Labora, Gómez-Serrano, Shi and Staffilani \[[24](#cite-ref24)\] removed the assumption of symmetry, for both systems, on $\mathbb R^3$ and on the <!-- source-page: 6 --> torus. Chen, Cialdea, Shkoller and Vicol \[[31](#cite-ref31)\] proved that the vorticity of smooth solutions of the two-dimensional compressible Euler equations can blow up, through an axisymmetric implosion that is stable in finite codimension in its radial part and for an open set of swirl velocities; see \[[30](#cite-ref30)\] for every dimension $d\ge3$, and \[[36](#cite-ref36)\] for a family of smooth non-isentropic implosions of the compressible Euler equations whose ground state is stable without symmetry up to finitely many conditions on the data. Buckmaster and Iyer \[[19](#cite-ref19)\] constructed shocks for the two-dimensional compressible Euler equations that converge in self-similar variables to an unstable self-similar solution of the Burgers equation, and showed that this behavior is stable modulo a two-dimensional subspace.

For the incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb R^3$, Elgindi \[[47](#cite-ref47)\] constructed self-similar solutions of class $C^{1,\alpha}$, for some $\alpha>0$, that blow up in finite time, and Elgindi, Ghoul and Masmoudi \[[48](#cite-ref48), Theorem 2\] proved that this blow-up is stable in a class of axisymmetric perturbations, up to one condition on the perturbation, which gives blow-up from data of finite energy. For the nonlinear heat equation in one space dimension, Bricmont and Kupiainen \[[15](#cite-ref15), Theorems 1 and 2\] constructed solutions that blow up with a prescribed profile by fixing finitely many parameters of the data, one for each unstable direction of the profile as a fixed point of a renormalization map, and for the Navier–Stokes equations with complex-valued solutions, Li and Sinai \[[71](#cite-ref71)\] proved blow-up in finite time for suitable values of the parameters in ten-parameter families of data. For the energy supercritical heat equation, Collot, Raphaël and Szeftel \[[38](#cite-ref38), Theorem 1.2\] proved that there is a Lipschitz manifold of finite codimension of data without symmetry whose solutions blow up near a self-similar profile, up to scaling and translation; these data are the profile, cut off at a large radius, plus a small perturbation.

On $\mathbb T^3$ we construct the solution for a small blow-up time $T$. By the scaling of the equations this is the same as a large period at the blow-up time $1$: if $u$ solves the equations on $[0,1)\times\mathbb R^3/L\mathbb Z^3$, then $L\,u(L^2 t,Lx)$ solves them on $[0,L^{-2})\times\mathbb T^3$. We therefore keep the solution $u^*$ and the blow-up time $1$, and we take the period $L=T^{-1/2}$ large. The solution $u^*$ is not periodic, so that on the torus there is no exact solution about which to linearize, and no monodromy operator. We cut the field $u^*$ off at the radius $r=L/8$ and extend it periodically: the approximate solution is $u^{\mathrm a}(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z^3}\bar u(t,\cdot-Lj)$, where $\bar u(t)$ is the cutoff field above for this radius, which equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{L/16}$ and vanishes outside $B_{L/8}$. On divergences the heat flow composed with the Leray projection is the convolution with a kernel that decays like $|x|^{-4}$, uniformly in time. The nonlinear term is a divergence, and so is the datum, since a divergence-free field $f$ is the divergence of $x\otimes f$. Hence the flows of the datum and of the nonlinear term on $\mathbb R^3$ differ from those of their periodic extensions on the torus, on a period cell, by quantities of order $L^{-1/2}$ and $L^{-5/2}$ in $\dot H^1$ (Lemma 6.1), and with the bound for the cutoff the error by which $u^{\mathrm a}$ fails to be a solution is of order $L^{-1/2}$ (Lemma 6.2). For the linearized problem we use that $\bar u(t)$ vanishes outside $B_{L/8}$, so that in the equation linearized about $u^{\mathrm a}$ the term that comes from $u^{\mathrm a}$ involves the perturbation only through its restriction <!-- source-page: 9 --> to this ball. We can therefore solve the linearized equation on $\mathbb R^3$, with the right inverse of the equation linearized about $u^*$, and return to the torus; the map so obtained inverts the equation linearized about $u^{\mathrm a}$ up to an error of order $L^{-1/2}$. A Neumann series removes this error when $L$ is large. The same contraction as on $\mathbb R^3$ then gives a solution $u$ on the torus of period $L$, and $u_{\mathrm{per}}(t,x)=L\,u(L^2 t,Lx)$ is the solution of Theorem 1.1.

changes.note: Organizes finite symmetry, time-translation corrections and forward Navier–Stokes instability by how each mechanism differs from tracking the blow-up profile.
changes.adapted_text:
Finite rotational symmetry imposes quite different restrictions in two and three dimensions. Elgindi and Jeong \[[49](#cite-ref49)\] proved global existence and uniqueness for two-dimensional Euler with bounded vorticity invariant under rotation by $2\pi/m$, $m\ge3$, even without decay at infinity. In three dimensions their octahedrally symmetric construction on $\mathbb R^3$ gives finite-time blow-up from bounded, piecewise smooth vorticity \[[50](#cite-ref50)\]. <!-- source-page: 5 --> Drivas and Elgindi \[[45](#cite-ref45), Problem 6\] ask whether scale-invariant Euler solutions can become singular within an admissible symmetry class. The rotating surface quasi-geostrophic solutions in \[[25](#cite-ref25)\] have threefold symmetry.

For nonlinear wave equations, Donninger and Schörkhuber \[[43](#cite-ref43)\], following \[[42](#cite-ref42)\] on wave maps, used the Lyapunov–Perron method to correct the unstable time-translation direction and then absorbed the correction by moving the blow-up time. This is the method that we use, except that we keep the modification of the data. Glogić, Hilditch and Wallauch \[[57](#cite-ref57)\] proved finite-codimensional stability of discretely self-similar blow-up for a wave maps type equation.

For Navier–Stokes, forward instability can separate two solutions with the same datum. Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] gave a spectral condition on a forward self-similar profile sufficient for nonuniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions. Following Vishik’s work on two-dimensional Euler \[[91](#cite-ref91), [92](#cite-ref92), [4](#cite-ref4)\], Albritton, Brué and Colombo \[[2](#cite-ref2)\] proved forced Leray–Hopf nonuniqueness. In the unforced case Buckmaster, Coiculescu and Li \[[17](#cite-ref17)\] followed a growing Floquet mode of a forward discretely self-similar solution. Here we follow the stable directions toward the blow-up time, and the solution converges to the profile. Other mechanisms give nonunique finite-energy weak solutions by convex integration \[[20](#cite-ref20), [18](#cite-ref18), [21](#cite-ref21)\], or two global solutions on the torus, smooth at positive times, from one $BMO^{-1}$ datum \[[37](#cite-ref37)\].
changes.authors_text:
In the certificate the symmetries restrict the perturbations for which the estimates are required (Section 7). Classes of fields with a discrete rotational symmetry have been used for the Euler equations. Elgindi and Jeong \[[49](#cite-ref49)\] proved that the two-dimensional Euler equations have a unique global solution with bounded vorticity for every bounded initial vorticity, without decay at infinity, that is invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/m$ for some $m\ge3$, and in \[[50](#cite-ref50)\] they proved the formation of a singularity in finite time for the three-dimensional Euler equations <!-- source-page: 5 --> on $\mathbb R^3$ in the class of the fields with octahedral symmetry, for data with bounded, piecewise smooth vorticity. Problem 6 of the survey of Drivas and Elgindi \[[45](#cite-ref45)\] asks whether a scale-invariant solution of the Euler equations in a symmetry class that is admissible in their sense can develop a singularity in finite time. The rotating solutions of the surface quasi-geostrophic equation of \[[25](#cite-ref25)\] (see Subsection 1.2) have a 3-fold symmetry.

For wave equations, Donninger and Schörkhuber \[[43](#cite-ref43)\] proved the stability of a self-similar blow-up by the Lyapunov–Perron method, following the work of Donninger on wave maps \[[42](#cite-ref42)\]: the data are modified along the unstable direction, which there comes from the translations in time, and the modification is undone at the end by a shift of the blow-up time. This is the method that we use, except that we keep the modification of the data. Glogić, Hilditch and Wallauch \[[57](#cite-ref57)\] constructed discretely self-similar blow-up solutions of a wave maps type equation and proved their stability in finite codimension.

Non-unique solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations have been produced by several methods. One is convex integration: Buckmaster and Vicol \[[20](#cite-ref20)\] proved that weak solutions with finite kinetic energy are not unique; see also \[[18](#cite-ref18)\] and the survey \[[21](#cite-ref21)\]. Another is that of Coiculescu and Palasek \[[37](#cite-ref37)\], who constructed, for the equations on the torus, data in $BMO^{-1}$ with two distinct global solutions, both smooth at positive times, by a mechanism proposed for a dyadic model of the equations. A third is based, like the proofs of blow-up recalled above, on the linearization about a self-similar solution in self-similar variables. Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] proved that Leray–Hopf solutions are not unique if the linearization about a forward self-similar solution satisfies a spectral condition. After the work of Vishik on the two-dimensional Euler equations \[[91](#cite-ref91), [92](#cite-ref92), [4](#cite-ref4)\], Albritton, Brué and Colombo \[[2](#cite-ref2)\] proved the non-uniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions with a force, and Buckmaster, Coiculescu and Li \[[17](#cite-ref17)\] proved it without force, around a forward discretely self-similar solution whose linearization has a growing Floquet mode. In these works an unstable direction of the linearized flow is followed forward in time, and the solutions separate. Here we follow the stable directions toward the blow-up time, and the solution converges to the profile.

In the proof of Theorem 7.1 we correct an approximate profile to an exact one. Since the period of a profile is not known in advance, we rescale the self-similar time, so that the period becomes a coefficient of the equation. The equation linearized about a time-periodic solution need not be invertible: it has, for instance, the derivative of the solution in time in its kernel. We therefore add to the first equation of (1.2) a force term with finitely many unknown coefficients and impose as many linear constraints on the solution. With the Fredholm alternative, the a priori estimate of a certificate gives a bounded inverse of the linearized problem with constraints. The approximate profiles depend on as many parameters as the force term has coefficients, and the remaining conditions bound these coefficients so sharply that the Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem, applied to the parameters and to the quadratic term together, gives a value of the parameters and a solution close to the approximate profile for which the force term vanishes. We then show that this solution is smooth (Proposition 7.11), and since its isometry is the identity, the theorem of Chae and Wolf recalled in Subsection 1.2 gives the Type I bound.

changes.adapted_text: *Computer-assisted construction of profiles.* Computer-assisted proofs first reduce a functional estimate to quantitative conditions and then enclose the numerical errors in checking those conditions \[[58](#cite-ref58)\]. Chen and Hou \[[32](#cite-ref32), [33](#cite-ref33)\] used such a reduction for blow-up from smooth data in the two-dimensional Boussinesq and three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler equations with boundary. Earlier work with Huang treated the De Gregorio and Hou–Luo models \[[34](#cite-ref34), [35](#cite-ref35)\]. Other applications include the smooth imploding profiles of \[[16](#cite-ref16)\] and the one-dimensional kernel in Castro, Córdoba and Gómez-Serrano’s construction of rotating surface quasi-geostrophic solutions \[[25](#cite-ref25)\]. <!-- source-page: 7 --> The closest periodic constructions are for Navier–Stokes with time-independent forcing on the torus \[[90](#cite-ref90)\] and in a square \[[9](#cite-ref9)\], and for discrete self-similarity in the Einstein–scalar field system \[[80](#cite-ref80)\] and the defocusing nonlinear wave equation \[[22](#cite-ref22)\]. The discussion entitled [Related constructions](#sec-related-constructions) at the end of Subsection 7.10 compares their methods with Section 7. Other computations locate candidate flows. Neural networks have produced approximate self-similar Euler and model profiles \[[93](#cite-ref93), [94](#cite-ref94)\]. Guillod and Šverák \[[59](#cite-ref59)\] found a symmetry-breaking bifurcation for forward self-similar Navier–Stokes solutions with large axisymmetric data. Ionescu, Jia and Palasek \[[63](#cite-ref63)\] computed unstable forward profiles in the axisymmetric class without swirl. Hou \[[61](#cite-ref61)\] reported numerical evidence of possible singularity for smooth finite-energy axisymmetric data.
changes.authors_text: Several results in fluid mechanics have computer-assisted proofs, in which an analytic argument reduces the statement to finitely many conditions and a computation with rigorous bounds for its errors verifies them; see the survey \[[58](#cite-ref58)\]. Chen and Hou proved in this way the blow-up of the two-dimensional Boussinesq and the three-dimensional axisymmetric Euler <!-- source-page: 7 --> equations from smooth data in a domain with boundary \[[32](#cite-ref32), [33](#cite-ref33)\], following their proofs with Huang of the finite-time blow-up, from smooth data, of the De Gregorio and Hou–Luo models of the three-dimensional Euler equations \[[34](#cite-ref34), [35](#cite-ref35)\]; the smooth imploding profiles of \[[16](#cite-ref16)\] are constructed with the help of a computer, and the global rotating solutions of the surface quasi-geostrophic equation of Castro, Córdoba and Gómez-Serrano \[[25](#cite-ref25)\] rest on a computer-assisted proof that the kernel of a linearized operator is one-dimensional. Time-periodic solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations with a time-independent force have been constructed in this way on the torus \[[90](#cite-ref90)\] and in a square \[[9](#cite-ref9)\], and so have discretely self-similar solutions of the Einstein–scalar field system \[[80](#cite-ref80)\] and of the defocusing nonlinear wave equation \[[22](#cite-ref22)\]. Such proofs start from approximate solutions computed numerically. Approximate self-similar solutions of the Euler equations and of related models have also been found by neural networks \[[93](#cite-ref93), [94](#cite-ref94)\]. For the Navier–Stokes equations, Guillod and Šverák \[[59](#cite-ref59)\] computed forward self-similar solutions for axisymmetric scale-invariant data and found a symmetry-breaking bifurcation at large data, and Ionescu, Jia and Palasek \[[63](#cite-ref63)\] constructed numerically unstable forward self-similar solutions in the axisymmetric class without swirl; Hou \[[61](#cite-ref61)\] presented numerical evidence of potentially singular behavior of axisymmetric solutions with smooth data of finite energy. We compare the construction of Section 7 with those of \[[90](#cite-ref90), [9](#cite-ref9), [80](#cite-ref80), [22](#cite-ref22)\] in Subsection 7.4.

changes.adapted_text: For comparison, the following Euler and porous-media constructions allow forcing of specified regularity. With a force that is uniformly of class $C^{1,\alpha}$, the construction of Elgindi gives the blow-up of solutions of the Euler equations of finite energy \[[47](#cite-ref47), Remark 1.4\], and Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa proved singularity formation for the Euler equations with a force that is uniformly of class $C^{1,1/2-\varepsilon}$ \[[39](#cite-ref39)\] and for the incompressible porous media equation with a source that is smooth in space \[[40](#cite-ref40)\]. For forces smooth in both space and time up to the singular time, see \[[7](#cite-ref7), [5](#cite-ref5), [6](#cite-ref6)\] for the incompressible porous media, Boussinesq and Euler equations, respectively. The construction in \[[8](#cite-ref8)\] gives unforced Euler blow-up from smooth periodic data.
changes.authors_text:
Theorem 1.1 concerns the equations with zero force. With a force that is uniformly of class $C^{1,\alpha}$, the construction of Elgindi gives the blow-up of solutions of the Euler equations of finite energy \[[47](#cite-ref47), Remark 1.4\], and Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa proved singularity formation for the Euler equations with a force that is uniformly of class $C^{1,1/2-\varepsilon}$ \[[39](#cite-ref39)\] and for the incompressible porous media equation with a source that is smooth in space \[[40](#cite-ref40)\]. Singularity formation was proved for the incompressible porous media, Boussinesq and Euler equations with forces that are smooth in space and time up to the singular time in \[[7](#cite-ref7), [5](#cite-ref5), [6](#cite-ref6)\], and for the Euler equations without force, from smooth periodic data, in \[[8](#cite-ref8)\].

The formalization also derives the conclusion of the formal Theorem 1.1, on $\mathbb R^3$ and on $\mathbb T^3$, from conditions on finitely many functions and numbers, which do not include the estimates that a certificate assumes for every perturbation. We describe these conditions in Appendix B. The formalization contains no data: that the certificate of Subsection 1.1 satisfies them is verified by a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic, which is not part of the formalization.

changes.note: Identifies the pressure whose gradient has zero mean, states the action of the projection, and gives the two proof routes.
changes.adapted_text:
For the passage from a profile to finite-energy data, Sections 2–6 prove Theorem 1.1. Section 3 gives the heat estimates, Section 4 chooses the initial correction, and Sections 5–6 localize the profile on the two domains. Appendix A supplies the auxiliary proofs, including smoothness (Lemma 2.3). For the construction of the profile, Section 7 can be read after Section 3. Appendix B gives the conditions on the represented data, and Appendix C describes the numerical search and the fields in Figure 1.

From Section 2 on, the solutions that we construct blow up at time $1$, except for the solution on $\mathbb T^3$, which is a dilation of one of them. The letters $s$ and $y$ are reserved for the self-similar variables. We write $\bar B_r$ for the closure of the ball $B_r$. For a field $f$ on $\mathbb R^3$ we write $|\nabla f|^2=\sum_i|\partial_i f|^2$, and similarly for derivatives of higher order. The Fourier transform is $\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,f(x)\,dx$, with inverse $\mathcal F^{-1}$, and the Fourier coefficients of a periodic function are $\hat f(k)=\int_{[0,1]^3}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x}\,f(x)\,dx$, $k\in\mathbb Z^3$. The Leray projection $\mathbb P$ removes the component parallel to each nonzero Fourier frequency. It therefore annihilates gradients at those frequencies. The gradient of a periodic pressure has zero mean, so the projection annihilates it on the torus as well. In Fourier variables $\mathbb P$ multiplies $\hat f(\xi)$, and on the torus $\hat f(k)$, by the matrix $\mathbb P_\xi=I-|\xi|^{-2}\,\xi\otimes\xi$, where $\mathbb P_0=I$, so that on the torus it keeps the mean.
changes.authors_text:
In Section 2 we reduce Theorem 1.1 to Propositions 2.1 and 2.2, on $\mathbb R^3$ and on the torus, and to Lemma 2.3 on smooth data. Section 3 contains the properties of the heat flow and of the bilinear term that the rest of the paper uses; most of its proofs, and that of Lemma 2.3, are in Appendix A. In Section 4 we construct the right inverse of the equation linearized about $u^*$ and prove the lemma by which a contraction corrects an approximate solution. In Section 5 we prove Proposition 2.1, and in Section 6 Proposition 2.2. In Section 7, which can be read after Section 3, we define a certificate and prove Theorem 7.1. In Appendix B we describe the form that the formalization prescribes for the data of a certificate, and we derive the estimates that a certificate assumes for every perturbation from conditions on finitely many functions and numbers, attached to data of this form. In Appendix C we describe the numerical computation of the field from which the approximate profiles of the certificate of Subsection 1.1 are formed, and of further fields of this certificate.

From Section 2 on, the solutions that we construct blow up at time $1$, except for the solution on $\mathbb T^3$, which is a dilation of one of them. The letters $s$ and $y$ are reserved for the self-similar variables. We write $\bar B_r$ for the closure of the ball $B_r$. For a field $f$ on $\mathbb R^3$ we write $|\nabla f|^2=\sum_i|\partial_i f|^2$, and similarly for derivatives of higher order. The Fourier transform is $\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,f(x)\,dx$, with inverse $\mathcal F^{-1}$, and the Fourier coefficients of a periodic function are $\hat f(k)=\int_{[0,1]^3}e^{-2\pi i k\cdot x}\,f(x)\,dx$, $k\in\mathbb Z^3$. The Leray projection $\mathbb P$ multiplies $\hat f(\xi)$, and on the torus $\hat f(k)$, by the matrix $\mathbb P_\xi=I-|\xi|^{-2}\,\xi\otimes\xi$, where $\mathbb P_0=I$, so that on the torus it keeps the mean.

We used Anthropic models (Claude) throughout this work, and no others. The work builds on unreleased work of the authors on computer-assisted proofs, in particular concerning the non-uniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions in the style of Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] and blow-up for fluid equations with boundary. It builds also on numerical work of the authors on finding self-similar profiles, on our earlier papers on singularity formation, and on our unreleased drafts on the forced hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations and the forced Navier–Stokes equations. The idea of pursuing discretely self-similar solutions came from the paper of the second author with Coiculescu and Li on non-uniqueness \[[17](#cite-ref17)\]. The agents were given a curated dossier of potential leads and then guidance after our strictly-uncontaminated experiment producing unforced Euler and forced Navier–Stokes blow-up from our forced Euler and forced hypodissipative Navier–Stokes manuscripts. A simpler mechanism sufficed to produce unforced hyperdissipative Navier–Stokes blow-up, i.e. for $\nu\cdot(-\Delta)^{\frac{501}{500}}$, and then a heavier computation produced this profile. We used the enslopification skills of Scott Armstrong \[[10](#cite-ref10)\] to create a draft from an initial Lean proof (Subsection 1.5); the draft followed that proof step by step. We then rewrote it with Claude under our direction, citing standard results in place of proofs and simplifying the argument over successive revisions, so that the proof given here no longer follows the Lean proof.

changes.adapted_text: *The authors’ formal statements.* The authors’ [formal development](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/tree/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean) (revision `ad53419`) follows an earlier proof in Lean 4 \[[41](#cite-ref41)\] with Mathlib \[[73](#cite-ref73)\]. Its profile hypothesis adds $|\nabla^2 W|+|\nabla q|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$ to (1.3). For every positive viscosity it gives smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free data on $\mathbb R^3$ for which there is no global smooth solution of bounded energy. It also gives smooth divergence-free periodic data for which there is no global smooth solution with periodic velocity. The data may depend on viscosity. Remark 1.2 supplies the velocity derivative bounds. The pressure-gradient decay is an additional hypothesis in this comparison. The authors’ certificate theorem constructs a nonzero weak recurrent profile. <!-- source-page: 10 --> *The quantitative statements.* A separate [formalization for this edition](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/blob/4e96459ec6e474314ea92274ab443093492c957e/lean-wrappers/navier-stokes-edition/lean/MainTheorems.lean#L47-L65) proves the whole-space rate and physical-variable error (1.6) under the formal decay hypotheses. Its [certificate theorem](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/blob/4e96459ec6e474314ea92274ab443093492c957e/lean-wrappers/navier-stokes-edition/lean/SectionSeven.lean#L23-L59) retains the selected parameter, the smooth symmetric profile and the bounds (7.38). The formal certificate requires, among other things, joint $C^1$ regularity of the approximate velocity and a specified decaying weak second spatial derivative. The written torus proof in Section 6 gives (1.7), which is an [open target](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/blob/4e96459ec6e474314ea92274ab443093492c957e/lean-wrappers/navier-stokes-edition/lean/OpenTargets.lean#L18-L54) in the edition’s formal development. The [original statement checks](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/actions/runs/44819023135) and the [edition checks at `4e96459`](https://github.com/wcook04/proof-reader/actions/runs/45023118802) record the compiled results. For a certified computation of water waves formalized in Lean see \[[82](#cite-ref82)\].
changes.authors_text: Theorems 1.1 and 7.1 have been formalized in the Lean 4 proof assistant \[[41](#cite-ref41)\], using its mathematical library Mathlib \[[73](#cite-ref73)\], in the form in which an earlier version of this paper stated them. The formal Theorem 1.1 has no rate: for every positive viscosity <!-- source-page: 10 --> it gives a smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free datum on $\mathbb R^3$ from which no smooth solution of bounded energy exists for all time, and a smooth, periodic, divergence-free datum from which no smooth solution with periodic velocity exists for all time. The formal Theorem 7.1 obtains from a certificate a weak solution of the equation of a profile. For another recent use of Lean in fluid mechanics, the verification of a certified computation of water waves, see \[[82](#cite-ref82)\].

changes.adapted_text: For a smooth solution with periodic velocity, (1.1) makes $\nabla p$ periodic. The increment of $p$ across each unit period is therefore spatially constant. Writing the three increments as $b(t)$ gives $p(t,x)-b(t)\cdot x$ periodic. Take $a''(t)=-b(t)$ with $a(0)=a'(0)=0$. The velocity $u(t,x+a(t))-a'(t)$ solves (1.1) with pressure $p(t,x+a(t))+a''(t)\cdot x$. This change of frame preserves the datum and gives periodic pressure, as Fefferman requires \[[53](#cite-ref53), Errata, unnumbered PDF p. 6\].

changes.adapted_text: To see the consequence for Fefferman’s formulation, suppose the compactly supported datum above had a smooth finite-energy solution through time $1$. On the closed interval $[0,1]$ this solution has bounded $H^1$ norm by Tao \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 11.1, preprint p. 68\], since its initial velocity is in $H^1$ and the force is zero. Its velocity is that of an $H^1$ mild solution \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 4.3, preprint p. 28\]. Uniqueness \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4, preprint pp. 33–34\] identifies it with $u$ for $t<1$, contrary to (1.6). On the torus, uniqueness for smooth periodic solutions with periodic pressure \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1, preprint pp. 28–29\] gives the same contradiction to (1.7).

changes.adapted_text: Three properties of the heat evolution enter the proof. The factor $\tau^{-3/4}$ in (3.7) is integrable at zero, so the quadratic term can be integrated up to the current time. At each positive lag the same operator is compact when one velocity is fixed (Lemma 3.2), which controls the part of the period map outside the free spectral disk in Section 4. On $\mathbb T_L^3$ the heat and Sobolev estimates retain constants independent of $L$, as required for the passage to large period in Section 6. Appendix A.1 proves Lemmas 3.3–3.7. We write $\lesssim$ for an inequality up to a constant, absolute in this section and in Appendix A unless otherwise specified.
changes.authors_text: In this section we collect the properties of the heat flow and of the bilinear term $K$ that are used below. Lemma 3.1 is classical; we prove Lemma 3.2 here and Lemmas 3.3–3.7 in Appendix A.1. Here and below the symbol $\lesssim$ denotes an inequality that holds up to a constant factor. In this section and in Appendix A the constant is absolute, unless we say what it depends on.

changes.adapted_text:
The fields $u\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $
abla u\in L^2$ form the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the norm $\|
abla u\|_{L^2}$, and the Sobolev inequality $$ egin{equation}
\|u\|_{L^6}\lesssim\|
abla u\|_{L^2}	ag{3.1}
\end{equation}$$ follows componentwise from the scalar inequality \[[56](#cite-ref56), (II.3.11), p. 56\]. To approximate a field in $L^6$ with gradient in $L^2$, cut it off at radius $R$ and then mollify. For a cutoff $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ equal to one on $B_R$ and zero outside $B_{2R}$, the extra gradient term is bounded in $L^2$ by $\|u\|_{L^6(B_{2R}\setminus B_R)}\|
abla\chi_R\|_3$, which tends to zero since the second factor is independent of $R$. This scalar cutoff gives density in the ambient space. Divergence zero defines a closed subspace, so $X$ is a real Hilbert space. On $\mathbb R^3$, every field in $X$ can be approximated in the gradient norm by smooth compactly supported divergence-free fields \[[60](#cite-ref60), Theorem 8, p. 89; definitions on pp. 64–65\]. This last density statement is what allows the spectral correction in Subsection 4.4 to have compact support.

changes.note: Explains how localization of one factor and compactness on a ball give a compact operator at fixed positive lag.
changes.adapted_text:
At a fixed lag $\tau>0$, one factor in $K(\tau)$ can be approximated by a compactly supported field. The remaining factor is then needed only on a bounded ball, where Rellich compactness applies. This makes the monodromy operator of Subsection 4.3 a compact perturbation of a contraction.

*Proof.* Fix $\tau>0$. By (3.7), approximating $u$ from $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ approximates $K(\tau)(u,\cdot)$ in operator norm. Compact operators are closed in that norm. It is thus enough to prove $\|K(\tau)(\varphi,v_k)\|_{\dot H^1}\to0$ for $\varphi\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ and $v_k\rightharpoonup0$ in $X$.
changes.authors_text:
The next lemma is the property of $K$ that makes the monodromy operator of Subsection 4.3 a compact perturbation of a contraction.

*Proof.* Let $\tau>0$. By (3.7) the operator $K(\tau)(u,\cdot)$ depends continuously on $u\in X$ in the operator norm, and $C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ is dense in $X$. It therefore suffices to prove that $\|K(\tau)(\varphi,v_k)\|_{\dot H^1}\to0$ for every $\varphi\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ and every sequence $(v_k)$ that converges weakly to $0$ in $X$.

changes.note: Explains why bounded restriction and compact embedding give convergence of the full weakly null sequence.
changes.adapted_text:
Let $B$ be a ball that contains the support of $\varphi$. For $v\in X$ the matrix field $F_v=\varphi\otimes v+v\otimes\varphi$ vanishes outside $B$, and $\operatorname{div}F_v=(v\cdot\nabla)\varphi+(\varphi\cdot\nabla)v$, because $v$ and $\varphi$ are divergence-free; thus $K(\tau)(\varphi,v)=-\tfrac12\,e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}F_v$. Since $|\widehat{\operatorname{div}F_v}(\xi)|\le2\pi|\xi|\,|\hat F_v(\xi)|$ and $16\pi^4|\xi|^4e^{-8\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\le\tau^{-2}$, the definition (2.2), the last identity of (3.2) and Plancherel’s identity give $$
\|K(\tau)(\varphi,v)\|_{\dot H^1}^2=\frac14\int 4\pi^2|\xi|^2e^{-8\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}\bigl|\mathbb P_\xi\widehat{\operatorname{div}F_v}(\xi)\bigr|^2\,d\xi\le\frac{\|F_v\|_{L^2}^2}{4\,\tau^2}\le\frac{\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}^2\|v\|_{L^2(B)}^2}{\tau^2}.
$$ Only the values on $B$ enter the last bound. By (3.1) and $\|v\|_{L^2(B)}\le |B|^{1/3}\|v\|_6$, restriction to $B$ is continuous from $X$ to $H^1(B)$, so $v_k\rightharpoonup0$ there. Rellich’s theorem on the bounded ball gives compactness in $L^2(B)$ \[[14](#cite-ref14), Theorem 9.16, p. 285\]. Every subsequence thus has a further subsequence converging strongly to its weak limit, zero. The last bound now gives convergence of $K(\tau)(\varphi,v_k)$ in $X$. $\square$

For fields in $L^2_tE_2$, Furioli, Lemarié-Rieusset and Terraneo proved the distributional formulation with a pressure equivalent to the integral formulation \[[55](#cite-ref55), Definition 2 and Proposition 1, p. 607\]; Dubois proved that both are equivalent to formulations without a pressure, tested against divergence-free fields \[[46](#cite-ref46), Theorem 1, pp. 29–30\]. Testing against solenoidal fields removes $\nabla p$ by integration by parts. Dubois’s result then recovers the projected integral equation for the velocity in the stated class. changes.adapted_text:
Every $t\in[0,1)$ is $t_n+\lambda^n\sigma$ for some $n\ge0$ and $\sigma\in[0,t_1)$. Then $\lambda^{n+1}<1-t\le\lambda^n$, and $\|u^*(t)\|_{\dot H^1}=\lambda^{-n/4}\,\|u^*(\sigma)\|_{\dot H^1}$ by (4.3) and (3.5). Hence (4.4) holds with $$
C=\max_{[0,t_1]}\|u^*\|_{\dot H^1},\qquad c_*=\lambda^{1/4}\min_{[0,t_1]}\|u^*\|_{\dot H^1},
$$ provided $u^*$ vanishes at no time. If $u^*(a)=0$, uniqueness in Lemma 3.5 gives $u^*=0$ on every $[a,b]$, $a<b<1$. Every earlier time advances into $[a,1)$ under (4.3); since its dilation and isometry are invertible, $u^*$ would vanish everywhere on $[0,1)$, contrary to Proposition 4.1. Continuity on $[0,t_1]$ then makes the displayed minimum positive. $\square$

changes.adapted_text:
Let $P$ be the Riesz projection for the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$ \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, (1.6)–(1.8), p. 244\]. It commutes with $\mathcal M$ and has finite rank, the sum of the finite algebraic multiplicities \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, Paragraph 1.17, pp. 246–247\]. Complex conjugation commutes with $\mathcal M$ and preserves this spectral set; conjugating the resolvent integral therefore leaves $P$ unchanged. Hence $P$ preserves the real space $X$; denote its restriction by $P_{\mathrm u}$. The subscript labels every mode exterior to $|z|=\Theta$, including the slowly decaying ones. The spectra of the restrictions of $\mathcal M$ to $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ and to $\operatorname{ran}P$ are the parts of the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ in $\{|z|<\Theta\}$ and in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$. Hence the first restriction has spectral radius less than $\Theta$, and the second is invertible, with an inverse of spectral radius less than $\Theta^{-1}$; in particular $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ is invertible. The spectral radius formula \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter III, Exercise 1.17(2), p. 167\] gives geometric bounds with ratios $r_{\mathrm s}<\Theta$ for forward powers and $r_{\mathrm b}<\Theta^{-1}$ for inverse powers. After the weights in (4.11), their ratios are $r_{\mathrm s}/\Theta<1$ and $\Theta r_{\mathrm b}<1$, so both series converge. $\square$

In this subsection $\Theta$, $P_{\mathrm u}$ and $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ are those of Lemma 4.5, and $\kappa$ is defined by $\lambda^\kappa=\Theta$; then $0<\kappa<\tfrac14$, because $\lambda^{1/4}<\Theta<1$. The next lemma restricts the inhomogeneous mild equation to the intervals $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$ and rescales each of them to $[0,t_1]$. The additive term $g$ is a trajectory in the integral equation. Subtracting $g$ before restarting gives the heat evolution of $(v-g)(t_n)$ on the next interval. The same background $u^*$ then appears on every rescaled interval by (4.3).

Let $P$ be the Riesz projection of $\mathcal M$ for the part of its spectrum in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$ \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, (1.6)–(1.8)\]. It commutes with $\mathcal M$, it has finite rank \[[51](#cite-ref51), Chapter IV, Paragraph 1.17\], and it maps $X$ into $X$, because $\mathcal M$ is a real operator and $I-P$ is the integral of $(2\pi i)^{-1}\,(z-\mathcal M)^{-1}$ over the circle $|z|=\Theta$; let $P_{\mathrm u}$ be the restriction of $P$ to $X$. The spectra of the restrictions of $\mathcal M$ to $\operatorname{ran}(I-P)$ and to $\operatorname{ran}P$ are the parts of the spectrum of $\mathcal M$ in $\{|z|<\Theta\}$ and in $\{|z|>\Theta\}$. Hence the first restriction has spectral radius less than $\Theta$, and the second is invertible, with an inverse of spectral radius less than $\Theta^{-1}$; in particular $\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}$ is invertible. By the spectral radius formula the two series of (4.11) converge. $\square$

*Proof.* Lemma 3.4, with $f=u^*$, gives a continuous solution of (4.12) on each $[0,b]$, $b<1$. Uniqueness makes these solutions agree on overlaps, giving the unique solution on $[0,1)$. The map $v-g$ has the value $\chi$ at time $0$, so that $\chi_0=\chi$. By (4.12) and by (3.13), applied on the same intervals with $u=v-g$, $f=2u^*$ and $h=v$, $$
(v-g)(t)=e^{(t-t_n)\Delta}(v-g)(t_n)+2\int_{t_n}^t K(t-t')(u^*(t'),v(t'))\,dt'\qquad(t_n\le t<1).
$$ We apply $\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}$ to this identity at time $t=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma$. On the left we obtain $v_n(\sigma)-g_n(\sigma)$. In the first term on the right, $\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}e^{\lambda^n\sigma\Delta}=e^{\sigma\Delta}\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}$, by (3.5) and since $\rho_R$ commutes with the heat flow and with the dilations; thus this term becomes $e^{\sigma\Delta}\chi_n$. In the integral we substitute $t'=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma'$. By the last two identities of (3.8) and by (4.3), in the form $\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}u^*(t_n+\lambda^n\sigma')=u^*(\sigma')$, $$
\lambda^n\rho_R^{-n}D_{\lambda^n}K\bigl(\lambda^n(\sigma-\sigma')\bigr)\bigl(u^*(t'),v(t')\bigr)=K(\sigma-\sigma')\bigl(u^*(\sigma'),v_n(\sigma')\bigr)\qquad(0\le\sigma'<\sigma),
$$ so that the integral becomes $\mathcal B(u^*,v_n)(\sigma)$. Therefore $$
v_n=e^{t\Delta}\chi_n+2\mathcal B(u^*,v_n)+g_n\quad\text{on }[0,t_1],\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad v_n=\mathcal U(e^{t\Delta}\chi_n+g_n)=h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal Ug_n.
$$ Since $t_n+\lambda^nt_1=t_{n+1}$, we have $v_{n+1}(0)=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda v_n(t_1)$ and $g_{n+1}(0)=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda g_n(t_1)$, so that $$
\chi_{n+1}=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda(h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal Ug_n-g_n)(t_1)=\mathcal M\chi_n+f_n,
$$ by (4.10) and the definition (4.13) of $f_n$.
