changes.note: Explains why density gives exact preimages and why the lift has a bounded inverse. Identifies the reason for lifting the finite-dimensional projection into compactly supported fields, then gives the finite-dimensional argument.
changes.adapted_text: *Proof of Proposition 4.3.* The spectral projection prescribes $P_{\mathrm u}\gamma$, whereas Sections 5 and 6 require $\gamma$ itself to have compact support. We can meet both requirements. Since $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ is dense and $P_{\mathrm u}$ is continuous, its image on this class is dense in $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$. This linear image is closed by finite dimensionality, so every basis vector in the range has a compactly supported smooth solenoidal preimage. Their span $E$ makes $P_{\mathrm u}|_E$ an isomorphism. Its bounded inverse gives $\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\|P_{\mathrm u}\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$. Constants may depend on the fixed choices of $\Theta$, $\kappa$, $P_{\mathrm u}$ and $E$.
changes.authors_text: *Proof of Proposition 4.3.* We first fix $E$. Since $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ is dense in $X$ (Subsection 3.1) and $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$ has finite dimension, $P_{\mathrm u}$ maps $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ onto $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$. We choose fields of $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$ that $P_{\mathrm u}$ maps to the elements of a basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$, and we let $E$ be their linear span. Then $P_{\mathrm u}$ maps $E$ isomorphically onto $\operatorname{ran}P_{\mathrm u}$, so that $\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\|P_{\mathrm u}\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$ for $\gamma\in E$. The numbers $\Theta$ and $\kappa$, the projection $P_{\mathrm u}$ and the space $E$ are chosen once, and the constants in $\lesssim$ depend on them.

changes.note: Uses the first occurrence of each forcing term in the recurrence to explain the exponent m+1 and the sign of the initial correction.
changes.adapted_text:
Fix $g\in C_\kappa([0,1);X)$. Its forcing terms $f_m$ are independent of the datum (Lemma 4.6). In (4.14), $P_{\mathrm u}f_m$ first contributes to $\chi_{m+1}$. Pull it back $m+1$ periods to time zero. By (4.15) the resulting term has norm $\lesssim\Theta^{m+1}\|\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m+1)}P_{\mathrm u}\|\,\|g\|_\kappa$, so these terms are summable by (4.11). The Lyapunov–Perron choice cancels their sum with $P_{\mathrm u}\gamma$. Since $P_{\mathrm u}|_E$ is an isomorphism, this determines exactly one $\gamma\in E$ with $$
P_{\mathrm u}\gamma=-\sum_{m\ge0}\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m+1)}P_{\mathrm u}f_m,\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}\lesssim\|g\|_\kappa.
$$ We take $\chi=\gamma$ in Lemma 4.6. Since $P_{\mathrm u}$ commutes with $\mathcal M$, the recursion gives, by induction on $n$, $$
P_{\mathrm u}\chi_n=-\sum_{m\ge n}\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-(m-n+1)}P_{\mathrm u}f_m,\qquad
(I-P_{\mathrm u})\chi_n=\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\gamma+\sum_{m<n}\mathcal M^{n-1-m}(I-P_{\mathrm u})f_m.
$$ <!-- source-page: 21 --> We bound the terms of the two sums by (4.15), with $m=n-1+j$ in the first sum and $m=n-1-j$ in the second: $$
\begin{aligned}
\|P_{\mathrm u}\chi_n\|_{\dot H^1}&\lesssim\Theta^{n-1}\|g\|_\kappa\sum_{j\ge1}\Theta^j\|\mathcal M_{\mathrm u}^{-j}P_{\mathrm u}\|,\\
\|(I-P_{\mathrm u})\chi_n\|_{\dot H^1}&\lesssim\|\mathcal M^n(I-P_{\mathrm u})\|\,\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}+\Theta^{n-1}\|g\|_\kappa\sum_{0\le j<n}\Theta^{-j}\|\mathcal M^j(I-P_{\mathrm u})\|.
\end{aligned}

*Proof.* Let $C$ be the constant of Lemma 4.7, and let $\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$. By (4.20), $e^{t\Delta}\chi\in C_\kappa([0,1);\mathcal X)$. Let $\delta=2\,C_{\mathcal R}\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$, so that $2C\,C_{\mathcal R}\delta\le\frac12$ by (4.23). For $v'$ in the closed ball of radius $\delta$ of $C_\kappa([0,1);\mathcal X)$ let $\Phi(v')$ be the second component of $$
\mathcal R\bigl[e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B(v',v')\bigr].
$$ By (4.22) and (4.19), $$
\|\Phi(v')\|_\kappa\le C_{\mathcal R}\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa+C\,C_{\mathcal R}\delta^2\le\frac\delta2+\frac\delta4,
$$ and since $\mathcal R$ is linear and $\mathcal B(v',v')-\mathcal B(v'',v'')=\mathcal B(v'-v'',v')+\mathcal B(v'',v'-v'')$, the map $\Phi$ is Lipschitz on the ball with constant $2C\,C_{\mathcal R}\delta\le\frac12$. The ball is complete by the identification following (4.5), and the preceding estimate makes it invariant under $\Phi$. The contraction principle gives a fixed point $v$ there, with (4.24). Let $\gamma$ be the first component of $\mathcal R[e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B(v,v)]$, whose second component is $v$. Then $(\gamma,v)$ satisfies (4.17), by (4.22), and the last assertion follows from the equivalence stated before (4.17). $\square$

*Proof.* Fix $r>0$ and $0\le t<1$; all constants below are independent of $r$ and $t$. Differentiation under the integral over $[0,1]$, locally in $(t,x)$ with $t<1$, gives the smoothness of $A$ and $\bar u$. Since $u^*(t)$ is divergence-free, $$
\operatorname{curl}_x[\sigma\,u^*(t,\sigma x)\times x]=\partial_\sigma[\sigma^2\,u^*(t,\sigma x)],
$$ and integration in $\sigma$ gives $\operatorname{curl}A(t)=u^*(t)$: the term at $\sigma=0$ vanishes because of the factor $\sigma^2$. The product rule gives $$
\bar u(t)=\eta(\cdot/r)\,u^*(t)+r^{-1}(\nabla\eta)(\cdot/r)\times A(t).
$$ Thus $\bar u(t)$, which is divergence-free as a curl, equals $u^*(t)$ on $B_{r/2}$, where $\eta(\cdot/r)=1$, and vanishes outside $B_r$; in particular it belongs to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$.

\bar u(t)=\eta(\cdot/r)\,u^*(t)+r^{-1}(\nabla\eta)(\cdot/r)\times A(t).

C_{\mathcal R}^2\,\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon_1,\qquad4\,C_{\mathcal R}\,\varepsilon_0\le c_*.
$$ For $w_0\in X$ within $\varepsilon_0$ of $W(0)$ in $\dot H^1$, put $\chi=w_0-u^*(0)$. By (1.4) and (4.20), $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le\|\chi\|_{\dot H^1}\le\varepsilon_0$. Since $u^*$ solves the equation (Proposition 4.1), only the heat evolution of $\chi$ enters (4.23). The first condition on $\varepsilon_0$ permits the contraction of Lemma 4.8 with $u^{\mathrm a}=u^*$, $J:E\hookrightarrow X$ and right inverse (4.8). It gives $\gamma\in E$ and $v\in C_\kappa([0,1);X)$ with $u=u^*+v$ a solution on $[0,1)$ and $u(0)=w_0+\gamma$. By (4.24) and the second condition on $\varepsilon_0$, $$
\|u(t)-u^*(t)\|_{\dot H^1}=\|v(t)\|_{\dot H^1}\le2\,C_{\mathcal R}\,\varepsilon_0(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}\le\tfrac12\,c_*(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}\qquad(0\le t<1).

We look for a solution in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ on $[0,1)$ of the following form, where $\Pi_L$ denotes $L$-periodization (Subsection 6.1). We take $L$ large enough that every $\gamma\in E$ fits inside the support ball $B_{L/8}$ (Subsection 6.3). $$
u=u^{\mathrm a}+z,\qquad u(0)=u^{\mathrm a}(0)+\Pi_L\gamma,
$$ Here $\gamma\in E$ and $z\in C_\kappa([0,1);\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3))$. The field $u^{\mathrm a}$ is the periodization of the curl of the cutoff potential at radius $L/8$. On $B_{L/16}$ it agrees with $u^*$. Its residual in the periodic integral equation has weighted norm $O(L^{-1/2})$ (Lemma 6.2). There is also a linear error. When we use the whole-space inverse to solve the periodic linearized equation with right-hand side $g$, the defect has norm $O(L^{-1/2})\|g\|_\kappa$ (Lemma 6.3). For large $L$ the Neumann series removes the linear defect. With this exact right inverse, Lemma 4.8 removes the nonlinear residual.

Let $x\in\mathbb R^3$ with $\max_i|x_i|<\frac L2$, let $x'\in\bar B_{L/8}$ and $j\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}$. With $|j|_\infty=\max_i|j_i|$ we have $|x-x'-Lj|\ge L\,|j|_\infty-\frac58L\ge\frac38L\,|j|_\infty$, and since $F$ vanishes almost everywhere outside $\bar B_{L/8}$, we obtain $$
|h(x-Lj)|\lesssim\bigl(L\,|j|_\infty\bigr)^{-4}\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad|\nabla h(x-Lj)|\lesssim\bigl(L\,|j|_\infty\bigr)^{-5}\|F\|_{L^1}.
$$ There are $O(n^2)$ lattice points with $|j|_\infty=n$. The shells therefore give summable bounds $\lesssim L^{-4}n^{-2}\|F\|_{L^1}$ and $\lesssim L^{-5}n^{-3}\|F\|_{L^1}$. Thus $g_0=\sum_{j\ne0}h(\cdot-Lj)$ and its first derivatives converge uniformly on $\max_i|x_i|<\frac L2$, with $$
|g_0|\lesssim L^{-4}\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad|\nabla g_0|\lesssim L^{-5}\|F\|_{L^1}.
$$ To identify $g_0$, compare Fourier coefficients. Since $h\in L^1$, its periodization has coefficients $L^{-3}\hat h(k)$, where $\hat h(k)=e^{-4\pi^2t|k|^2}\,\mathbb P_k\,\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k)$ by (2.2) and (3.10). Periodization gives $\operatorname{div}\Pi_LF$ the coefficients $L^{-3}\widehat{\operatorname{div}F}(k)$, so Subsection 3.6 gives precisely the same coefficients for its projected heat flow. Fourier uniqueness therefore gives $e^{t\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\Pi_LF=h+g_0$, that is, $g=g_0$ and $\nabla g=\nabla g_0$, almost everywhere on the cube. Since the cube has volume $L^3$, the bounds for $g_0$ give $$
\|g\|_{L^6(Q_L)}\lesssim L^{1/2}L^{-4}\|F\|_{L^1},\qquad\|\nabla g\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim L^{3/2}L^{-5}\|F\|_{L^1},
$$ which is (6.2). $\square$

Since $u^*=e^{t\Delta}u^*(0)+\mathcal B(u^*,u^*)$ and $\mathcal B$ is bilinear, $$
\bar F=(\bar u-u^*)-e^{t\Delta}\bigl(\bar u(0)-u^*(0)\bigr)-\mathcal B(\bar u-u^*,\bar u)-\mathcal B(u^*,\bar u-u^*).
$$ By (6.4), $\bar u-u^*$ is continuous and bounded by $CL^{-1/2}$ in $X$. Since $0<\kappa<1/4$, the weight $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}$ in (4.5) is at most one. Estimate the four terms by (6.4), (4.20), and twice (4.21), using the symmetry of $\mathcal B$ and $\bar u,u^*\in C_0([0,1);X)$. This gives $$
\|\bar F\|_\kappa\lesssim L^{-1/2}\bigl(1+\|\bar u\|_0+\|u^*\|_0\bigr)\lesssim L^{-1/2}.
$$ It remains to pass to the torus. Since $\bar u(t')$ is divergence-free, $(\bar u(t')\cdot\nabla)\bar u(t')=\operatorname{div}\bigl(\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')\bigr)$, and $(\Pi_L\bar u\cdot\nabla)\Pi_L\bar u=\Pi_L[(\bar u\cdot\nabla)\bar u]$. Hence the definitions (2.3) and (3.17) give $$
\begin{aligned}
\bar F(t)&=\bar u(t)-e^{t\Delta}\bar u(0)+\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')\bigr)\,dt',\\
F^{\mathrm a}(t)&=\Pi_L\bar u(t)-e^{t\Delta}\Pi_L\bar u(0)+\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\Pi_L\bigl(\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')\bigr)\,dt'.
\end{aligned}
$$ Here $\bar F$ is a whole-space field and $F^{\mathrm a}$ is periodic. Both vanish at $t=0$. For $0<t<1$ we restrict each to $Q_L$, where $\Pi_L\bar u(t)=\bar u(t)$. The field $\bar u(0)$ and the matrix fields $\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')$ are smooth and vanish outside $\bar B_{L/8}$. We apply (6.3) to the second terms, and Lemma 6.1 to the third terms under the integrals: $$
\|\nabla\bigl(F^{\mathrm a}(t)-\bar F(t)\bigr)\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim L^{-5/2}\|\bar u(0)\|_{L^1}+L^{-7/2}\int_0^t\|\bar u(t')\|_{L^2}^2\,dt'\lesssim L^{-1/2}.
$$ Indeed, support and (6.4) give $\|\bar u(0)\|_1\le|B_{L/8}|^{1/2}\|\bar u(0)\|_2\lesssim L^2$ and $\|\bar u(t')\otimes\bar u(t')\|_1=\|\bar u(t')\|_2^2\lesssim L$. The two contributions are therefore $O(L^{-1/2})$ and $O(L^{-5/2})$. Since $\|F^{\mathrm a}(t)\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}=\|\nabla F^{\mathrm a}(t)\|_{L^2(Q_L)}$, $$
\|F^{\mathrm a}(t)\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}\le\|\bar F(t)\|_{\dot H^1}+\|\nabla\bigl(F^{\mathrm a}(t)-\bar F(t)\bigr)\|_{L^2(Q_L)}\lesssim(1-t)^{\kappa-\frac14}L^{-1/2}+L^{-1/2},
$$ and multiplication by $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$ and the supremum in (4.5) give $\|F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa\lesssim L^{-1/2}$. Lemmas 3.7 and 3.3 give its continuity with values in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$. $\square$

changes.adapted_text: *Theorem 7.1 in brief.* If the approximate family satisfies the certificate conditions, one member can be corrected to a smooth, nonzero solution of the unforced similarity equation. The exact profile has the selected period and symmetries and lies within a prescribed $\dot H^1$ distance at every phase. The parameters here select the profile. Sections 4–6 separately adjust the initial velocity of a solution that tracks it; the two correction spaces can have different dimensions.

The proof is the argument described at the end of Subsection 1.3, in which we correct an approximate profile to an exact one.

changes.authors_text:
The computer-assisted constructions of time-periodic solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations with a time-independent force \[[90](#cite-ref90), Section 2\], \[[9](#cite-ref9), Section 2\] and of discretely self-similar solutions \[[80](#cite-ref80)\], \[[22](#cite-ref22), Section 1.3.1\] rescale the time, so that the period, or the frequency, becomes a coefficient of the equation, and impose a condition that removes the translations in time; see also the framework of \[[54](#cite-ref54), Section 3.3\], in which the frequency is an unknown and a phase condition is imposed. In these works the period is found together with the solution, by a fixed point argument around an approximate solution computed numerically, and symmetries reduce the problem, as the set $\Gamma$ does here: a group of sixteen elements in \[[90](#cite-ref90)\], a change of sign after half a period in \[[22](#cite-ref22)\]; for the certificate of Subsection 1.1, a rotation by $\pi/19$ about an axis after half a period and a rotation by $\pi$ about a perpendicular axis (Subsection B.1, with $\varkappa=19$). Here the constraints play the role of the condition on the translations, and the parameter, of which the period $S(\alpha)$ is a given function, is found together with the solution by the Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem (Proposition 7.10).

A force in a fixed finite span, with as many linear constraints, is used in \[[89](#cite-ref89)\] for patterns of the Swift–Hohenberg equation on a two-dimensional torus. There the force lies in the span of the derivatives of an approximate solution in the directions of translation, and its coefficients are shown to vanish by pairing the equation with the derivatives of the solution: by the invariance of the energy under translations, this gives a linear system for the coefficients \[[89](#cite-ref89), Theorem 2.6\], whose matrix is then verified to be invertible. Here the pairing with the fields $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ only bounds the coefficients of the force, as stated after (7.30). In the certificate of Subsection 1.1 only one of the forcing fields accounts for the translations in time; the others were computed as directions in which the inverse of the linearized operator is largest (Subsection C.4). In the construction by Donninger and Schörkhuber \[[44](#cite-ref44), Section 2.3\] of a self-similar blow-up solution of the cubic Schrödinger equation, where there is one parameter, the parameter is found after the solution: a term in the direction of a fixed function is added to a formal inverse of the linearized operator, <!-- source-page: 36 --> the modified equation is solved by a contraction for every small value of the parameter, and the coefficient of the added term vanishes at some value, by the intermediate value theorem.

Bounds for the inverse of a linearized operator, of which the a priori estimate (7.18) is an instance, are obtained by computer for stationary problems in several ways: by a decomposition into a coercive part and a compact part approximated by an operator of finite rank, as in \[[62](#cite-ref62), Section 3\] for the Navier–Stokes equations in forward self-similar variables on $\mathbb R^3$, where the strategy of Chen and Hou \[[32](#cite-ref32)\] is followed; by enclosures of eigenvalues, as in \[[95](#cite-ref95), Chapter 3\] for the stationary Navier–Stokes equations on an unbounded strip with an obstacle; and by an approximate inverse built from Fourier series on a box \[[23](#cite-ref23)\].

The rest of this section contains the proof of Theorem 7.1; a certificate is fixed throughout. The constants of the certificate are written out in every estimate that leads to one of its conditions. The other constants, denoted by $C$ or implied by the symbol $\lesssim$, depend only on $C_{\mathrm a}$, unless we say otherwise, and they enter none of the conditions.

$$ where all fields are taken at time $\theta$. The term in brackets is the left-hand side of (7.22) with $u=v(\theta)$. This $u$ is admissible in (7.22): for almost every $\theta$ it belongs to $X$ and $\Delta u\in L^2$, and <!-- source-page: 41 --> for every $(R,0)\in\Gamma$ the identity $\rho_Rv(\theta)=v(\theta)$ holds for almost every $\theta$, by the $\Gamma$-invariance of $v$, and therefore for every $\theta$, by the continuity of $v$. By (7.22), for almost every $\theta$, $$
 \frac1{2S}\mathcal E'(\theta)\leq\Lambda(\theta),\qquad
 \Lambda(\theta)=\Bigl(\|F(\theta)\|_{L^2}+\Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i b_i(\theta)\Bigr\|_{L^2}\Bigr)\|\Delta v(\theta)\|_{L^2}+c_3|v(\theta)|_w^2.
$$ The function $\Lambda$ is nonnegative, since $c_3\geq0$, and has period 1. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, by (7.9) and since $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}\leq\|v\|_w$, $$\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1\Lambda\,d\theta\leq\bigl(\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+b_*|\beta|\bigr)\|v\|_w+c_3\|v\|_w^2.
 \tag{7.56}
\end{equation}$$ Let $\theta_1$ be a point at which $\mathcal E$ attains its minimum. Then $$
 \mathcal E(\theta_1)\leq\int_0^1\mathcal E\,d\theta=\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}^2\leq\frac1{w_*}\|v\|_w^2,
$$ because $w\geq w_*$. The period of $\mathcal E$ is $1/m$. For $m=1$ this is already known. For $m=2$, (7.6) gives $R$ with $(R,\tfrac12)\in\Gamma$, and the $\Gamma$-invariance (7.5) of $v$ gives $v(\theta+\tfrac12)=\rho_Rv(\theta)$, first almost everywhere and then everywhere by continuity; $\rho_R$ preserves the $X$ norm. Thus, for $\theta\in[\theta_1,\theta_1+\frac1m]$, $$
 m\bigl(\mathcal E(\theta)-\mathcal E(\theta_1)\bigr)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\Bigl[\mathcal E\bigl(\theta+\tfrac km\bigr)-\mathcal E\bigl(\theta_1+\tfrac km\bigr)\Bigr]\leq2S\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\int_{\theta_1+k/m}^{\theta+k/m}\Lambda\,d\theta'\leq2S\int_0^1\Lambda\,d\theta',
$$ because the intervals have disjoint interiors, $\Lambda\ge0$, and its integral over any interval of length $1$ is the same. Periodicity of $\mathcal E$ then gives $$
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathbb R}\mathcal E(\theta)\leq\frac1{w_*}\|v\|_w^2+\frac{2S}m\int_0^1\Lambda\,d\theta,
$$ and (7.55) follows from (7.56). $\square$

 \mathcal G(\alpha,g)=\bigl(\mathcal N(\alpha'),\,(v\cdot\nabla)v\bigr),

changes.adapted_text: Give $\mathcal K$ its Euclidean topology and $\mathcal Z$ its weak topology. The latter is a closed ball in the closed subspace of $\Gamma$-invariant fields in the separable Hilbert space $\mathcal H$. Hence $\mathcal Z$ is weakly compact \[[14](#cite-ref14), Corollary 3.22, p. 71\] and metrizable \[[14](#cite-ref14), Theorem 3.29, p. 74\]. The product $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ is compact, convex and nonempty in $\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal H$ with $\mathcal H$ weak. Schauder–Tychonoff \[[88](#cite-ref88), §2, p. 770\] gives a fixed point once $\mathcal G$ is sequentially continuous. Let $\alpha_k\to\alpha$ and $g_k\rightharpoonup g$ in $\mathcal H$ with pairs in $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ and corresponding solutions $(v_k,\beta_k)$ and $(v,\beta)$. By continuity of $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $\mathcal N$ it suffices to show $\beta_k\to\beta$ and $(v_k\cdot\nabla)v_k\rightharpoonup(v\cdot\nabla)v$ in $\mathcal H$.

changes.authors_text: We claim that $\mathcal G$ has a fixed point. The set $\mathcal Z$ is a closed ball of the closed subspace of $\Gamma$-invariant fields in $\mathcal H$. Hence it is convex and compact for the weak topology of $\mathcal H$, and on $\mathcal Z$ this topology is metrizable, because $\mathcal H$ is separable \[[14](#cite-ref14), Corollary 3.22 and Theorem 3.29\]. Thus $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ is a compact convex subset of the locally convex space $\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal H$, in which $\mathcal H$ carries its weak topology, and by the Schauder–Tychonoff fixed point theorem \[[88](#cite-ref88), §2\] every continuous map of such a set into itself has a fixed point. Since the topology of $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ is metrizable, and since $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $\mathcal N$ are continuous, it remains to prove the following. Let $(\alpha_k,g_k)$ and $(\alpha,g)$ be points of $\mathcal K\times\mathcal Z$ such that $\alpha_k\to\alpha$ and $g_k\to g$ weakly in $\mathcal H$, and let $(v_k,\beta_k)$ and $(v,\beta)$ be the solutions at $(\alpha_k,g_k)$ and at $(\alpha,g)$. Then $\beta_k\to\beta$ in $\mathbb R^n$ and $(v_k\cdot\nabla)v_k\to(v\cdot\nabla)v$ weakly in $\mathcal H$.

$$ Split $\beta\cdot\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ as $V_j\cdot\beta+\beta\cdot(\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j)$. Bound the quadratic term by (7.32). Cauchy–Schwarz in $\mathbb R^n$ bounds the coefficient error; Cauchy–Schwarz in $\mathbb R^2$ combines it with $a_j\|v\|_w$ using the two components $\|v\|_w$ and $\omega|\beta|$. Applying (7.59) yields $$
 \begin{aligned}
 \bigl|V_j\cdot\beta+\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}+\bigl(Y(\alpha)\,\bar\ell(\alpha)\bigr)_j\bigr|
 &\leq a_j\,\|v\|_w+\frac{|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j|}{\omega}\,\omega\,|\beta|+\tilde a_j\,\|v\|_w^2\\
 &\leq\Bigl(a_j^2+\frac{|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j|^2}{\omega^2}\Bigr)^{1/2}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}+\tilde a_j\,\|v\|_w^2\\
 &\leq2\varepsilon\Bigl(a_j^2+\frac{|\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-V_j|^2}{\omega^2}\Bigr)^{1/2}+\tilde a_j\,(2\varepsilon)^2.
 \end{aligned}
$$ Now $$
 \begin{aligned}
 V_j\cdot(\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta)-d_j\alpha_j
 &=\Bigl[V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-\bigl(Y(\alpha)\,\bar\ell(\alpha)\bigr)_j-d_j\alpha_j\Bigr]\\
 &\quad+\Bigl[V_j\cdot\beta+\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}+\bigl(Y(\alpha)\,\bar\ell(\alpha)\bigr)_j\Bigr].
 \end{aligned}
$$ The first bracket has absolute value at most $o_j$ by (7.34), and the second has the bound just obtained. Their sum is bounded by the left side of (7.35), hence by $|d_j|\varrho_j$. This is the first inequality of (7.61).

changes.adapted_text:
We first prove the mild identity on every $[a,b]$ with $a<b<1$. The local integrability assumptions on $\mathcal W$, the chain rule (7.41) and $(u\cdot\nabla)u(t,x)=e^{3S\theta/2}(\mathcal W\cdot\nabla)\mathcal W(\theta,y)$ give local integrability of $\partial_tu$, $\Delta u$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u$. For $\phi\in C_c^\infty((-\infty,1))$ and $\psi\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$, the transformed test $e^{-S\theta}\phi(t)\psi(x)$ is smooth, divergence-free and compactly supported: the time support stays away from $t=1$. Since $dx\,dt=S e^{-5S\theta/2}\,dy\,d\theta$, testing the weak equation gives $$
 \begin{aligned}
 &\int_{-\infty}^1\phi(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl[\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u\bigr]\cdot\psi\,dx\,dt\\
 &\qquad=S\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\bigl[\mathcal T_S\mathcal W+(\mathcal W\cdot\nabla)\mathcal W\bigr](\theta,y)\cdot e^{-S\theta}\phi(t)\,\psi(x)\,dy\,d\theta=0.
 \end{aligned}
$$ Since $u(t)$ is divergence-free, an integration by parts on the left-hand side gives $$
 \int_{-\infty}^1\phi'(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(t)\cdot\psi\,dx\,dt=-\int_{-\infty}^1\phi(t)\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u(t)\cdot\Delta\psi+\bigl(u(t)\otimes u(t)\bigr):\nabla\psi\Bigr]\,dx\,dt.
$$ Both time-dependent pairings are continuous, since $u$ is continuous into $X\hookrightarrow L^6$ and $\psi$ has compact support. The identity says that the distributional derivative of the left pairing is the continuous right pairing in (3.14). Subtracting an antiderivative leaves a distribution with zero derivative, hence a constant. The original continuous pairing is therefore continuously differentiable and satisfies (3.14) at every $t<1$. Lemma 3.6 gives the mild identity on $[a,b]$.

changes.adapted_text: Fix $a<b<1$. By (7.65) and $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{L^1}\lesssim\tau^{-1/2}$ from (3.9), (7.64) converges absolutely pointwise and Fubini identifies it almost everywhere with the $X$-valued integral. Translating $a$ to zero gives the Stokes formula \[[69](#cite-ref69), (3.5), preprint p. 7\] with datum $u(a)$, force $-\sum_m\partial_m(u_m u)$ and kernel $\partial_m(O_\tau)_{ij}$. Thus $u(a+t,x)$ is a bounded mild solution with bounded datum \[[69](#cite-ref69), Section 4, preprint p. 10\]. Proposition 4.1 \[[69](#cite-ref69), preprint p. 11\] bounds the distributional derivatives $(t-a)^{k/2+l}\nabla_x^k\partial_t^l u$ on $(a,b)\times\mathbb R^3$ for all integers $k,l\geq0$. Starting earlier gives bounded derivatives of every order on each compact interval, hence a smooth representative of $u$ on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Its slices represent $u(t)$ in $X$ for every $t$ by continuity from almost every time.
changes.authors_text: We now prove that $u$ is smooth. Let $a<b<1$. By (7.65), $u$ is a bounded measurable function on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, and $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{L^1}\lesssim\tau^{-1/2}$, by (3.9). Hence, for every $t\in(a,b]$, the integral in (7.64) converges absolutely at every point of $\mathbb R^3$, and by Fubini’s theorem (7.64) holds almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^3$ with the integral taken at each point. With the time 0 in place of $a$, this is the formula \[[69](#cite-ref69), (3.5)\] for the solution of the Stokes system with the datum $u(a)$ and the right-hand side $-\sum_m\partial_m(u_m\,u)$: the kernel of that formula is the derivative $\partial_m$ of the kernel of $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P$, that is, $\partial_m(O_\tau)_{ij}$. Thus the bounded function $(t,x)\mapsto u(a+t,x)$ on $(0,b-a)\times\mathbb R^3$ is a mild solution of the Cauchy problem for (1.1) with the bounded datum $u(a)$, in the sense of \[[69](#cite-ref69), Section 4\], and by \[[69](#cite-ref69), Proposition 4.1\], for all integers $k,l\geq0$ the function $(t-a)^{k/2+l}\,\nabla_x^k\partial_t^l u$ is bounded on $(a,b)\times\mathbb R^3$, where the derivatives are taken in the sense of distributions. Since $a<b<1$ are arbitrary, $u$ is equal almost everywhere on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ to a smooth function, all derivatives of which are bounded on $[a,b]\times\mathbb R^3$ whenever $a<b<1$. For every $t<1$ the value of this function at time $t$ is the element $u(t)$ of $X$: this holds for almost every $t$, and both depend continuously on $t$. From now on $u$ denotes this smooth function.

changes.note: Expand the pressure reconstruction directly from solenoidal testing and verify the sign of the displayed radial primitive.
changes.adapted_text:
Set $G=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, which is smooth. Equation (3.14) gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}G(t)\cdot\psi\,dx=0$ for every compactly supported solenoidal test $\psi$ and every $t<1$. Taking $\psi$ to be the curl of a compactly supported smooth field gives $\operatorname{curl}G(t)=0$. The radial primitive on $\mathbb R^3$ then gives $G=-\nabla p$ with $$
 p(t,x)=-\int_0^1G(t,\sigma x)\cdot x\,d\sigma,
$$ which is smooth in $(t,x)$. To check the gradient, use $\partial_iG_j=\partial_jG_i$ and differentiate under the integral: the resulting integrand is $\partial_\sigma(\sigma G_i(t,\sigma x))$. Thus $\partial_i p=-G_i$, and $(u,p)$ satisfies (1.1) throughout $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$.
changes.authors_text:
We turn to the pressure. Let $G=\partial_tu-\Delta u+(u\cdot\nabla)u$, a smooth field on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Since $u$ is smooth, the identity (3.14) gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}G(t)\cdot\psi\,dx=0$ for every $t<1$ and every $\psi\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$, so that $\operatorname{curl}G(t)=0$ and $G=-\nabla p$ with $$
 p(t,x)=-\int_0^1G(t,\sigma x)\cdot x\,d\sigma,
$$ a smooth function on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$. Thus the smooth functions $u$ and $p$ satisfy (1.1) on $(-\infty,1)\times\mathbb R^3$.

changes.adapted_text: *Related constructions.* For time-periodic Navier–Stokes solutions with a prescribed, time-independent force, \[[90](#cite-ref90), (2.8)–(2.14), pp. 7–9 of the preprint\] treats the frequency as an unknown in a space-time Fourier expansion and fixes the phase. In \[[9](#cite-ref9), (2.14)–(2.15), p. 5\] the phase condition is imposed after rescaling time. Discretely self-similar constructions \[[80](#cite-ref80), Section 1.1, p. 5 of the preprint\], \[[22](#cite-ref22), Section 1.3.1, pp. 4–5\] and the general formulation \[[54](#cite-ref54), Section 3.3, (16)–(17), p. 8 of the preprint\] likewise find the orbit and its frequency or period together near an approximation. Symmetry reduces the unknowns, with sixteen elements in \[[90](#cite-ref90), p. 3, and §5.2, (5.6), p. 43 of the preprint\] and a half-period sign change in \[[22](#cite-ref22), Section 1.3.1, p. 4\]. For the data in Appendix B with $k_{\mathrm{rot}}=19$, a half-period time shift gives a rotation by $\pi/19$ about one axis. Rotation by $\pi$ about a perpendicular axis is a purely spatial symmetry. The constraints include a choice of time phase, while Proposition 7.10 selects $S(\alpha)$ together with the correction.

changes.adapted_text: For Swift–Hohenberg patterns on a two-dimensional torus, \[[89](#cite-ref89), (2.3), p. 4\] also adds a force in a fixed finite span and the same number of constraints. The forcing fields are translation derivatives of the approximate solution. Translation invariance of the energy makes pairing with derivatives of the exact solution a homogeneous linear system for the forcing coefficients; Theorem 2.6, p. 7, of \[[89](#cite-ref89)\] sets those coefficients to zero once its matrix is invertible. Here the pairings with $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ give the bounds following (7.30). For the certificate of Subsection 1.1, one forcing field accounts for time translations and the others are computed directions in which the linearized inverse is largest (Subsection C.4). Donninger and Schörkhuber \[[44](#cite-ref44), Section 2.3, steps (5)–(8), pp. 8–9 of the preprint\] use one parameter for cubic Schrödinger blow-up: they regularize a formal inverse by adding a term along a fixed function, solve the modified equation by contraction at each small parameter, and then use the intermediate value theorem to make its added coefficient vanish.

For Navier–Stokes in forward self-similar variables on $\mathbb R^3$, \[[62](#cite-ref62), Section 3.2, Assumptions 2–3, pp. 19–20\] splits the operator into coercive and compact parts and approximates the latter by finite rank, following the strategy of Chen and Hou \[[32](#cite-ref32), Section 2.2, steps 5–6, p. 9 of the arXiv preprint\]. For flow on an unbounded strip with an obstacle, \[[95](#cite-ref95), Section 3.2, pp. 33–35; Section 6.2, (6.7)–(6.10), pp. 68–69, and Theorems 6.7–6.8, pp. 71–72\] obtains inverse bounds from spectral enclosures. The construction in \[[23](#cite-ref23), Section 3.2, (26)–(28), p. 13 of the preprint\] instead uses an approximate inverse represented by Fourier series on a box.

changes.adapted_text: *Proof of Lemma 3.3.* Bilinearity, continuity in $\tau$ and (3.12) make $(\tau,\chi,\chi')\mapsto K(\tau)(\chi,\chi')$ jointly continuous for $\tau>0$. For $a\leq t'<t$ the integrand is continuous and bounded by $C_K(t-t')^{-3/4}\max_{[a,b]}\|u\|_{\mathcal X}\max_{[a,b]}\|v\|_{\mathcal X}$, integrable since $3/4<1$. For continuity in $t$, extend $u,v$ by their endpoint values, put $\tau=t-t'$ and integrate over $(0,b-a)$ with zero integrand for $\tau>t-a$. For almost every $\tau$ the integrand is continuous at $t$ under the same bound. Dominated convergence includes $t=a$. $\square$

changes.authors_text: *Proof of Lemma 3.3.* Since $K(\tau)$ is bilinear and continuous in $\tau$, the bound of (3.12) shows that the map $(\tau,\chi,\chi')\mapsto K(\tau)(\chi,\chi')$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$. Hence the integrand is continuous in $t'\in[a,t)$, with norm at most $C_K\,(t-t')^{-3/4}\max_{[a,b]}\|u\|_{\mathcal X}\,\max_{[a,b]}\|v\|_{\mathcal X}$, and it is integrable. After the substitution $\tau=t-t'$ the continuity of the integral in $t$ follows by dominated convergence. $\square$

authors: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#2
changes.note: Spells out why the contraction proves the linearity and boundedness assertion as well as existence and uniqueness.
adapted: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#2
changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.4.* For $\beta>0$, equip $C([a,b];\mathcal X)$ with $\|h\|_\beta=\max_{a\leq t\leq b}e^{-\beta(t-a)}\|h(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$, an equivalent complete norm. Let $Lh$ denote the integral term in the lemma. Lemma 3.3 gives $Lh\in C([a,b];\mathcal X)$. By (3.12) and $e^{-\beta(t-a)}=e^{-\beta(t-t')}e^{-\beta(t'-a)}$, its operator norm is at most $$
 2C_K\max_{[a,b]}\|f\|_{\mathcal X}\int_0^\infty\tau^{-3/4}e^{-\beta\tau}\,d\tau,
$$ where the substitution $s=\beta\tau$ makes the integral a finite constant times $\beta^{-1/4}$. Choose $\beta$ so that $\|L\|_\beta<1$. Then $h\mapsto Lh+g$ has a unique fixed point, and the convergent series $(I-L)^{-1}=\sum_{j\geq0}L^j$ shows that $g\mapsto h$ is linear and bounded. Equivalence of norms gives the asserted supremum-norm bound. $\square$
replaced: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#2
changes.authors_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.4.* For $\beta>0$ we give the space of continuous maps $h:[a,b]\to\mathcal X$ the norm $\max_{a\leq t\leq b}e^{-\beta(t-a)}\|h(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$, which is equivalent to the supremum norm. By Lemma 3.3 the integral term of the equation of the lemma defines a linear map of this space into itself, and since $e^{-\beta(t-a)}=e^{-\beta(t-t')}e^{-\beta(t'-a)}$, the bound of (3.12) shows that the norm of this map is at most $$
 2C_K\max_{[a,b]}\|f\|_{\mathcal X}\int_0^\infty\tau^{-3/4}e^{-\beta\tau}\,d\tau,
$$ where the integral is a constant multiple of $\beta^{-1/4}$. For $\beta$ large the map is a contraction, which gives the lemma. $\square$

authors: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#3
changes.note: Identifies the exchange of a bounded operator with an integral and the bilinear identity used in uniqueness.
adapted: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#3
changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.5.* Apply $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ to the identity at time $m$. This bounded linear operator commutes with the Bochner integral, which is integrable by Lemma 3.3. The semigroup law (3.11) and the first identity in (3.12) give $$
 e^{(t-m)\Delta}u(m)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))\,dt',
$$ and subtracting this from the identity at $t$, then splitting the integral at $m$, gives (3.13). For uniqueness, suppose $u(a)=v(a)$. Symmetry and bilinearity give $K(\tau)(u,u)-K(\tau)(v,v)=K(\tau)(u+v,u-v)$. Thus $u-v$ satisfies Lemma 3.4 with $f=(u+v)/2$ and $g=0$. Its unique solution is zero. $\square$
replaced: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#3
changes.authors_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.5.* We apply the bounded operator $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ to the identity for $u$ at time $m$. By (3.11) and the first identity of (3.12), $$
 e^{(t-m)\Delta}u(m)=e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)+\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))\,dt',
$$ and subtracting this from the identity at time $t$ gives (3.13). For the uniqueness, let $u$ and $v$ be two solutions on $[a,b]$ with $u(a)=v(a)$. Since $K$ is bilinear and symmetric, the difference $u-v$ satisfies the equation of Lemma 3.4 with $\frac12(u+v)$ in place of $f$ and with $g=0$, and hence $u=v$. $\square$

We deduce the lemma from the local theory in $H^1$, in the form given by Tao \[[84](#cite-ref84), Section 5\], which concerns solutions in a smaller class. An $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ in the sense of \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 31\], without force and with a divergence-free datum $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, is a divergence-free field $\tilde u\in L^\infty([0,b];H^1(\mathbb R^3))\cap L^2([0,b];H^2(\mathbb R^3))$ which satisfies the integral equation \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] with the datum $u_0$; its pressure $\tilde p$ is determined by $\tilde u(t)$ at each time $t$, through the formula \[[84](#cite-ref84), (9)\]. The periodic $H^1$ mild solutions of \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 29\] are defined in the same way on the torus. We show that such a solution with the datum $u(0)$ coincides with $u$ as long as it exists, and that its norm in $H^1$ remains bounded. By the alternative of \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] between existence and blow-up in $H^1$, it then exists on $[0,b]$ for every $b<T$, and $u$ has the smoothness that \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] proves in this class.

changes.note: States the local square integrability required by Dubois and explains the passage from fixed spatial tests to time-dependent tests and from a distributional to an X-valued integral.
adapted: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#4
changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.6.* Translate time to set $a=0$. Let $E_2$ be the closure of the Schwartz functions in $\sup_x\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}$ \[[46](#cite-ref46), p. 29\]. Hölder’s inequality gives $\sup_x\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^6}$; approximation by $C_c^\infty$ therefore embeds $L^6$ continuously in $E_2$. By (3.1), $u\in C([0,b];E_2)$, hence $u\in L^2((0,m);E_2)$ for each $m<b$, as Dubois’s theorem requires. Let $\varphi$ be a smooth compactly supported field on $[0,m]\times\mathbb R^3$, divergence-free at each time. To differentiate $\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)$, split its increment into the change in $u$ with the test fixed and the change in the test. Apply (3.14) to the first part and continuity of $u$ in $L^6$ to the second. This gives the continuous derivative <!-- source-page: 48 --> $$
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u\cdot\bigl(\partial_t\varphi+\Delta\varphi\bigr)+\bigl(u\otimes u\bigr):\nabla\varphi\Bigr]\,dx.
$$ Integration from $0$ to $m$ gives Dubois’s formulation (NSW) at time $m$, with datum $u(0)$ \[[46](#cite-ref46), p. 29\], so $u$ solves (NSW) on $(0,b)$. Theorem 1 of \[[46](#cite-ref46), pp. 29–30\] then supplies a tempered distribution $v_0$ such that $$
 u(t)=e^{t\Delta}v_0-\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(u(t')\otimes u(t')\bigr)\,dt'\qquad(0\leq t<b)
$$ in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^3)$. Its continuous trace at $t=0$ gives $v_0=u(0)$. Since $u(t')\in L^6$, $\nabla u(t')\in L^2$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, Hölder’s inequality gives $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)=(u\cdot\nabla)u\in L^{3/2}$. By (2.2)–(2.3), the integrand after the minus sign is $-K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$. Lemma 3.3 gives its integral in $X$; testing against Schwartz fields, which act continuously on $X$ by (3.1), identifies it with the distributional integral. This proves (2.4) for $t<b$. Continuity of both sides in $X$, from Subsection 3.1 and Lemma 3.3, includes $t=b$. $\square$

changes.authors_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.6.* Translating the time, we may assume that $a=0$. Let $E_2$ be the space of \[[46](#cite-ref46)\], the closure of the Schwartz functions on $\mathbb R^3$ in the norm $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}$. Since $\|f\|_{L^2(x+B_1)}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^6}$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ is dense in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, this space contains $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, and by (3.1) $u$ is a continuous map from $[0,b]$ to $E_2$. Let $0<m<b$, and let $\varphi$ be a smooth, compactly supported field on $[0,m]\times\mathbb R^3$ that is divergence-free at each time. Since $u$ is continuous with <!-- source-page: 48 --> values in $L^6$, the hypothesis (3.14) for the fields $\psi=\varphi(t)$ and the product rule show that the function $t\mapsto\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)\,dx$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,m]$, with the derivative $$
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}\Bigl[u\cdot\bigl(\partial_t\varphi+\Delta\varphi\bigr)+\bigl(u\otimes u\bigr):\nabla\varphi\Bigr]\,dx.
$$ Integrating from 0 to $m$, we obtain the identity of the formulation (NSW) of \[[46](#cite-ref46)\] at the time $m$, with the datum $u(0)$; the fields $\varphi$ above are the test fields of that formulation. Thus $u$ is a solution of (NSW) on $(0,b)$, and by \[[46](#cite-ref46), Theorem 1\] there is a tempered distribution $v_0$ such that $$
 u(t)=e^{t\Delta}v_0-\int_0^t e^{(t-t')\Delta}\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\bigl(u(t')\otimes u(t')\bigr)\,dt'\qquad(0\leq t<b)
$$ in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^3)$. At $t=0$ this gives $v_0=u(0)$. The field $\operatorname{div}(u(t')\otimes u(t'))=(u(t')\cdot\nabla)u(t')$ belongs to $L^{3/2}$, so that the integrand is $-K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$, by (2.2) and (2.3), and since the Schwartz fields are continuous linear functionals on $X$, by (3.1), the integral is that of (2.4). Thus (2.4) holds for $0\leq t<b$, and it holds at $t=b$ because both of its sides are continuous on $[0,b]$ with values in $X$ (Subsection 3.1 and Lemma 3.3). $\square$

authors: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#5
changes.note: Explains the division by the norm and the use of strong continuity at every positive smoothing time.
adapted: A.1 Proofs of the lemmas of Section 3#5
changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 3.7.* Let $L>0$ and $\tau>0$, let $f\in L^{3/2}(\mathbb T_L^3)$ have mean zero, and let $z=e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf$. Since $|\hat z(k)|\leq e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}L^{-3}\|f\|_{L^1(Q_L)}$, the field $z$ is smooth; it is real and divergence-free, and it has mean zero. Thus $z$ belongs to $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$, and so does the field $\Psi=-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}z$, whose Fourier coefficients are $4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)$. Since $\mathbb P_k$ is a real symmetric matrix and $\mathbb P_k\hat z(k)=\hat z(k)$, Parseval’s identity and (3.15) give $$
 \int_{Q_L}\Psi\cdot f\,dx=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2e^{-4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}\hat z(k)\cdot\overline{\hat f(k)}=L^3\sum_k4\pi^2|k|^2|\hat z(k)|^2=\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2.
$$ Since $4\pi^2|k|^2\leq\tau^{-1}e^{4\pi^2\tau|k|^2}$, the norms of $\Psi$ in $L^2(Q_L)$ and in $\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)$ are at most $\tau^{-1/2}$ and $\tau^{-1}$ times $\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}$. By Hölder’s inequality and (3.18) for $\Psi$, $$
 \|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}^2\leq\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|\Psi\|_{L^2(Q_L)}^{1/2}\|\Psi\|_{L^6(Q_L)}^{1/2}\lesssim\tau^{-3/4}\|f\|_{L^{3/2}(Q_L)}\|z\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)},
$$ which gives (3.19), immediately if $z=0$ and otherwise by division by $\|z\|_{\dot H^1}$. The identity $e^{t\Delta}e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb Pf=e^{(t+\tau)\Delta}\mathbb Pf$ holds coefficient by coefficient. For continuity at $\tau_0>0$, write the field near $\tau_0$ as $e^{(\tau-\tau_0/2)\Delta}(e^{(\tau_0/2)\Delta}\mathbb Pf)$. The inner field lies in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T_L^3)$, so strong continuity of the heat flow applies from both sides of $\tau_0$.

changes.adapted_text:
*Proof of Lemma 2.3.* Let $u$ satisfy the first assertion, set $u_0=u(0)$ and fix $0<b<T$. Obtain a local $H^1$ mild solution $\tilde u$ from $u_0$ on $[0,b']$, $0<b'\leq b$, by \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(ii)\]. By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i)\], $\tilde u$ is continuous in $H^1$ and hence in $X$ by solenoidality and $H^1\subset L^6$. Lemma 3.3 integrates $K(t-t')(\tilde u(t'),\tilde u(t'))$ from \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] in $X$, continuously in $t$. Schwartz tests identify the distributional integral, and continuity in $X$ extends the identity to every time. Lemma 3.5 gives $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$. Since $u_0\in C_{c,\mathrm{div}}^\infty$ is Schwartz, $\tilde u,\tilde p$ are smooth on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$ with every time and space derivative bounded in $L^2$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(iv)\]. Equation (10) of \[[84](#cite-ref84)\] gives (1.1). Testing with $\tilde u$ and integrating by parts gives $\frac d{dt}\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=-2\|\nabla\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2$, since solenoidality cancels pressure and transport. Thus $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}$ and $$
 \|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}+\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\qquad(0\leq t\leq b').
$$ Continuity of $u$ into $X$ on $[0,b]$ bounds the right side independently of $b'$. If the maximal $H^1$ time were $T_*\le b$, Lemma 3.5 would give $\tilde u=u$ on each $[0,b']$ with $b'<T_*$. The displayed bound would contradict the blow-up alternative \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.8, published pp. 56–57\]. The smooth solution thus agrees with $u$ on $[0,b]$ and has $L^2$ norm at most $\|u_0\|_{L^2}$, for arbitrary $b<T$.
changes.authors_text:
*Proof of Lemma 2.3.* Let $u$ be as in the first assertion, let $u_0=u(0)$ and $0<b<T$, and let $\tilde u$ be an $H^1$ mild solution on an interval $[0,b']$, $0<b'\leq b$, with datum $u_0$. By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i)\] it is a continuous map from $[0,b']$ to $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and since its values are divergence-free and $H^1(\mathbb R^3)\subset L^6(\mathbb R^3)$, it is a continuous map from $[0,b']$ to $X$. Since $\operatorname{div}\tilde u=0$, the integrand of \[[84](#cite-ref84), (11)\] is $K(t-t')(\tilde u(t'),\tilde u(t'))$, so that the integral converges in $X$ as well, to the same field, and is continuous in $t$ with values in $X$, by Lemma 3.3. Both sides of the equation are therefore continuous in $t$ with values in $X$, so that it holds at every time. Thus $\tilde u$ is a mild solution on $[0,b']$, and $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$, by Lemma 3.5. Moreover, $u_0$ is a Schwartz field. Hence $\tilde u$ and $\tilde p$ are smooth on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$, and all their derivatives in $t$ and $x$ are bounded on $[0,b']$ with values in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(iv)\]. The formula \[[84](#cite-ref84), (10)\] is the integral form of (1.1), so that $(\tilde u,\tilde p)$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b']\times\mathbb R^3$ with datum $u_0$. By these bounds we may multiply (1.1) by $\tilde u$ and integrate by parts over $\mathbb R^3$, which gives $\frac d{dt}\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=-2\|\nabla\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}^2\leq0$. Hence $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{L^2}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}$ and, since $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,b']$, $$
 \|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\leq\|u_0\|_{L^2}+\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\qquad(0\leq t\leq b').
$$ By \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.8\], either there is an $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ with datum $u_0$, or there are $T_*\in(0,b]$ and a map $\tilde u$ from $[0,T_*)$ to $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ as $t\to T_*$, whose restriction to $[0,b']$ is an $H^1$ mild solution with datum $u_0$ for every $b'<T_*$. The second case does not occur, because the bound above holds on $[0,b']$ for every $b'<T_*$. Hence there is an $H^1$ mild solution on $[0,b]$ with datum $u_0$. As we have shown, it is the restriction of $u$ to $[0,b]$, it is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b]\times\mathbb R^3$, and its norm in $L^2$ does not exceed that of $u_0$. Since $b<T$ is arbitrary, this proves the first assertion.

changes.adapted_text: For smooth mean-zero solenoidal $u_0$ on $\mathbb T^3$, apply the periodic $H^1$ theory \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i),(ii),(iv)\] with $K_{\mathbb T}$ replacing $K$. Continuity in $H^1$ and preservation of the mean \[[84](#cite-ref84), (39)\] give continuity in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb T^3)$. Lemma 3.7 permits the use of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5, identifying this velocity with $u$. If the alternative \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.2\] gave blow-up at $T_*\leq b<T$, (3.16) would give $\|\tilde u(t)\|_{H^1}\lesssim\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$ for $t<T_*$, excluding blow-up. The solution is therefore smooth on $[0,b]$ by Theorem 5.1(iv), with periodic pressure by the periodic $H^1$ definition \[[84](#cite-ref84), p. 29\]. This holds for every $b<T$. $\square$
changes.authors_text: Now let $u$ be as in the second assertion, with the smooth datum $u_0$, and let $0<b<T$. The argument is the same, with the periodic $H^1$ mild solutions, whose velocity and pressure are periodic, with $K_{\mathbb T}$ in place of $K$, and with \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i) and (iv) and Corollary 5.2\] in place of \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.4(i) and (iv) and Corollary 5.8\]. The datum has mean zero, as the theory on the torus requires \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1\]. A periodic $H^1$ mild solution with this datum is a continuous map into $H^1(\mathbb T^3)$ \[[84](#cite-ref84), Theorem 5.1(i)\] whose values are divergence-free and have mean zero \[[84](#cite-ref84), (39)\], and hence a continuous map into $\dot H_{\mathrm{div}}^1(\mathbb T^3)$, and Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5 apply in this space by Lemma 3.7. The second case of \[[84](#cite-ref84), Corollary 5.2\] does not occur: in that case $\tilde u=u$ on $[0,T_*)$, and $\|u(t)\|_{H^1(\mathbb T^3)}\lesssim\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T^3)}$ for $0\leq t<T_*$, by (3.16). Hence the restriction of $u$ to $[0,b]$ is a smooth solution of (1.1) on $[0,b]\times\mathbb T^3$, and since $b<T$ is arbitrary, this proves the second assertion. $\square$

changes.authors_text: In this appendix we describe the form that the formalization (Subsection 1.5) prescribes for the data of a certificate, and we derive, from conditions on finitely many functions and numbers attached to data of this form, the estimates (7.18), (7.19) and (7.22) and the bounds (7.32) to (7.34). The result is Proposition B.14: data of this form that satisfy these conditions are a certificate in the sense of Section 7. We prove it here except for two statements, whose proofs are in the formalization and which we only describe: Proposition B.1, the inequality for a multiplier with which the a priori estimate (7.18) begins (Subsection B.2), and Proposition B.4, the inequalities for the cells of a mesh of the meridian plane, from which the rest of this estimate is assembled along a tree of matrices (Subsection B.3). In the formalization the two are stated for larger classes of perturbations and of right-hand sides. By the conditions of this appendix we mean those of Subsections B.1 to B.4 together with the further ones that are named after <!-- source-page: 50 --> Proposition B.14; together they are the hypothesis of the formal statement. The radial phase of Subsection B.1 and the weights of Subsection B.2 are explained in Appendix C.

Besides the inequalities displayed below, they give the coefficients and lower bounds in (B.16), enforce invariance of the cell matrices under constant pressure shifts, and specify the maps from global coordinates to cell coordinates. changes.adapted_text: For each amplitude, the $\sigma$ and $\eta$ partitions divide $[0,1]\times[-1,1]$ into rectangles. On each rectangle the amplitude is a complex polynomial. Across a common edge the two polynomial traces agree, as do their derivatives normal to that edge up to the prescribed order. The orders in $(\sigma,\eta)$ are $(2,1)$ for $\mathsf A$, $(1,2)$ for $\mathsf B$, $(2,2)$ for $\mathsf S$ and $(1,1)$ for $\mathsf T$. These matches keep all components of (B.7) and (B.8) continuously differentiable when a derivative in the formulas crosses a partition edge. In addition, $\mathsf S$ and $\mathsf T$ vanish at $\sigma=0$. The field (B.6) is then of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ and has period 1 in $\theta$; its second derivatives are bounded functions, which are the classical derivatives away from the spheres and the cones about the $y_3$ axis that correspond to the points of the partitions and away from the sphere $\sigma=\sigma_{\mathsf g}$. Continuity of the first derivatives across the interfaces makes this piecewise Hessian the weak Hessian. The set $\mathcal A$ contains $(-\iota,-l)$ with $(\iota,l)$, with the complex conjugate data, so that the terms of (B.6) come in conjugate pairs; and it contains $(\iota^\flat,l)$ with $(\iota,l)$, with $\mathsf A(\sigma,-\eta)$ and $-\mathsf B(\sigma,-\eta)$ in place of $\mathsf A(\sigma,\eta)$ and $\mathsf B(\sigma,\eta)$, while $\mathsf S$ and $\mathsf T$ are odd in $\eta$. With these relations the field is invariant under the second pair of (B.1), and it is invariant under the first because its harmonics are those of (B.2). It is therefore $\Gamma$-invariant, since every element of $\Gamma$ is composed of powers of these two pairs and of a translation of $\theta$ by an integer.

abla(q_\alpha- rac12|W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|^2)$, where $q_\alpha=q^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\,q^i$. Each $q^i$ is the real part of a finite sum of terms $E_{\iota,l}\,\sigma^{h_0}(1-\sigma)^h(1-\eta^2)^{h'}\mathsf P$, with the functions $E_{\iota,l}$ of (B.5) for the phase $f_\alpha$ and with continuous piecewise polynomials $\mathsf P$. Its piecewise polynomials are given in a basis of Hermite type: in each variable and on each interval of the partition, by their derivatives up to an order $D-1$ at the two ends and by finitely many further coefficients, where the integer $D$ exceeds by at least one the order to which they are joined. The forcing fields are also of the first kind: $b_i$ is a field of the form (B.6), with a length $\mathsf L_i$ and a radial phase of its own, with $\gamma=0$ and with piecewise polynomials that vanish for $\sigma\geq\sigma_i$, for a point $\sigma_i<1$ of their partitions. The radius is obtained from $\sigma=|y|/(|y|+\mathsf L_i)$; continuity includes the boundary sphere. The adjoint fields do not depend on $\alpha$ either: for $j\in\mathcal J$ and every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ the field $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is one field $\psi_j$ of the form (B.6), with one length, one radial phase and one function $\mathsf g$ for all $j$ and with $h\geq3$ in every term. There are two finite index sets $\mathcal P_\lambda$ and $\mathcal P_\mu$. Each index $p$ carries a harmonic set $\mathcal N_p$ disjoint from $-\mathcal N_p$, a rotation rate $
u_p(\alpha)$, a nonnegative weight $\lambda_p$ or $\mu_p$, a transport bound for $|W^{\mathrm r}+ rac12y-
u_p\mathbf e_z	imes y|$, and positive auxiliary functions. A $\mu$ index also carries a positive auxiliary number; there is a common $c_\mu\in(0,1)$. All these functions are axisymmetric. Before adding the $p$ terms, they are $\mathsf I_{2,\iota}=\mathsf D_\iota- rac3{50}$, $\mathsf I'_{2,\iota}=1-\mathsf D_\iota$, $\mathsf I'_{1,\iota}= rac14-\mathsf Z_\iota$, $\mathsf I_{1,\iota}=\mathsf Z_\iota-|
abla^2\mathsf D_\iota|_{\mathrm{op}}- rac3{50}w$ and $\mathsf I_{0,\iota}=-|
abla^2\mathsf Z_\iota|_{\mathrm{op}}$, where $|\cdot|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is the matrix operator norm. Thus $\mathsf D_\iota$ transfers part of the squared curl-gradient term to the Hessian term, and $\mathsf Z_\iota$ transfers part of the squared curl term to the gradient term. The Hessians of $\mathsf D_\iota$ and $\mathsf Z_\iota$ bound the costs of these transfers.

*The five coefficients in (B.16).* Start with the five baseline values above and add the following increments, one for each multiplier. Fix $y,\alpha,\iota$ and one multiplier $p$. Write $N=\mathcal N_p$, $\chi=\mathbf1_{\{\iota\in N\cup(-N)\}}$, $\omega_p=|\Omega_p(\iota)|$, $b$ for the relative transport bound and $\nu=\nu_p(\alpha)$. On the finite reference spectrum $H$, denote the bounds for the harmonics of $W^{\mathrm r},\nabla W^{\mathrm r},\operatorname{curl}W^{\mathrm r},\nabla\operatorname{curl}W^{\mathrm r}$ by $U_\beta,G_\beta,C_\beta,D_\beta$, respectively. Write $G_\Sigma=\sum_{\beta\in H}G_\beta$, and $C_*,D_*$ for the two bounds on the full reference vorticity and its gradient. For any one of these arrays $A$, set $$
 I_A=\sum_{\substack{\sigma=\pm1\\\sigma\iota\in N}}
       \ \sum_{\substack{\beta\in H\\\sigma\iota-\beta\notin N}}A_\beta,\qquad
 O_A=\sum_{\substack{\sigma=\pm1\\\sigma\iota\notin N}}
       \ \sum_{\substack{\beta\in H\\\sigma\iota+\beta\in N}}A_\beta .
$$ In $I_A$ the selected harmonic receives a coupling from outside $N$; in $O_A$ the reference harmonic carries it into $N$. Both sums run over the two signs, including when $\iota=0$. For either weight $a=\lambda_p$ or $\mu_p$, abbreviate $Q_d(a)=(ab+|\nabla a|)^2/(4d)$ and $J(a)=\mathbf1_{\{a+|\nabla a|>0\}}$. The increments are pointwise, with derivatives of Lipschitz weights understood almost everywhere.

For a curl multiplier write $a=\lambda_p$ and denote its positive auxiliary functions by $d,e,L,s_0,t_0,t_1,t_2,t_3$ (the two shares, length, scale and four Young parameters). Define $$
 B=|\nu|+\tfrac12\bigl((1+t_0)C_*+L D_*+
                 t_1 I_G+t_2 I_D+t_3 I_C\bigr).
$$ The Hessian coefficient $\mathsf I_2$ receives no increment. Suppressing the index $\iota$, the four others receive $$
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta\mathsf I'_2 &=-d\chi J(a)-e\,\mathbf1_{\{a>0\}}\,O_U/s_0,\\
 \Delta\mathsf I'_1 &=\chi\bigl(a\omega_p-Q_d(a)-a^2s_0I_U/(4e)-aB\bigr)
                         -aO_G/(2t_1),\\
 \Delta\mathsf I_1  &=-\tfrac a2(\chi C_*/t_0+O_C/t_3),\\
 \Delta\mathsf I_0  &=-\tfrac a2(\chi D_*/L+O_D/t_2).
\end{aligned}
$$ For a velocity multiplier write $a=\mu_p$, with positive share $d$, Young parameter $t_4$ and number $\eta>0$. Its only increments are $$
\begin{aligned}
 \Delta\mathsf I_1={}&-d\chi J(a)-aO_U/(2t_4),\\
 \Delta\mathsf I_0={}&\chi\bigl((1-c_\mu)a\omega_p-Q_d(a)-a|\nu|
                   -t_4aI_U/2-\eta a^2/2\bigr)\\
      &-\chi G_\Sigma(G_\Sigma-I_G)/(2\eta)-G_\Sigma O_G/(2\eta).
\end{aligned}
$$ For instance, a mode outside $\pm N$ receives no frequency gain from $p$. It can still lose part of its gradient coefficient through $O_U$ when a reference harmonic couples it into $N$. The [pointwise multiplier formulas](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Breakdown/Cert/CoerciveStatement.lean#L637-L710) use the pair (time frequency, angular frequency), which is $(2\iota_2-\iota_1,k_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1)$ in (B.2).

The data also obey a reflection symmetry. Under $(\iota,y)\mapsto(\iota^\flat,R_*y)$, permutations of the $\lambda$ and $\mu$ indices carry $\mathcal N_p$ to $\{\iota^\flat:\iota\in\mathcal N_p\}$ and $\nu_p$ to $-\nu_p$. The functions $\mathsf D_\iota,\mathsf Z_\iota$, the weights, transport and reference bounds, and auxiliary data are unchanged. The sign is preserved. So is $\Omega_p$: the time frequency $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ in (B.2) is unchanged under $\iota\mapsto\iota^\flat$, while the angle frequency and the rotation rate both change sign. Substitution in the coefficient formulas gives $$\begin{equation}
 \text{the coefficients of }\mathcal I_{\iota^\flat}\text{ at }R_*y\text{ are those of }\mathcal I_\iota\text{ at }y.
 \tag{B.17}
\end{equation}$$ The reflection identities for the piecewise coefficients hold off $y_3=0$, which suffices for (B.17) in the density integral.

On a cell that meets the axis only harmonics with $\iota_1=0$ are resolved. Each resolved harmonic of a cell has two degrees $\mathsf d_0\geq1$ and $\mathsf d\geq\mathsf d_0+2$, with $\mathsf d_0\geq2$ if it is the harmonic of a triple $\varphi$ on $\mathsf Q$, and the polynomials $\varphi_r$, $\varphi_\phi$, $\varphi_z$ of such a triple have degrees at most $(\mathsf d_0,\mathsf d_0-1)$, $(\mathsf d_0,\mathsf d_0)$ and $(\mathsf d_0-1,\mathsf d_0)$ in $(r,z)$.

changes.adapted_text: For each resolved harmonic the cell has finitely many unknowns, linear functionals of one mode of a perturbation and of its pressure in the cell: the coefficients of its gradient and of its components in products of orthonormal polynomials of degree at most $\mathsf d$ and $\mathsf d-1$ in each variable, moments of its traces and of the pressure on the sides, and values at corners. To these are added $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, a vector $\zeta\in\mathbb R^n$ and finitely many further unknowns. A trace of the perturbation or its associated pressure can occur in two neighbouring cells, so their local unknowns cannot be chosen independently. We use one real vector $x_{\mathrm g}=(x_{\mathrm p},x_{\mathrm f})$. The perturbation and the given coefficients $\beta$ fix $x_{\mathrm p}$. The free coordinates $x_{\mathrm f}$ include $\zeta$ and will be chosen in the proof of Proposition B.8. The matrix $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}$ reads off the unknowns for cell $\mathsf Q$ from this one vector. The matrices $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}$ are formed by relations that hold for every perturbation, such as the continuity of a trace across a side, the symmetry at the plane $z=0$, or the divergence equation on a side. The vectors of unknowns of a cell are complex, and $\langle\mathsf Ax,x\rangle$ denotes the real part of the form of a matrix $\mathsf A$ on a vector $x$.

To these are added $\beta\in\mathbb R^n$, a vector $\zeta\in\mathbb R^n$ and finitely many further unknowns. The unknowns of all the cells are expressed through two finite sets of real unknowns, the global unknowns, by a matrix $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}$ for each cell. Those of the first set are determined by a perturbation and include $\beta$; those of the second set, which we call *free*, include the $\zeta_i$. We write $x_{\mathrm g}=(x_{\mathrm p},x_{\mathrm f})$ for a real vector of global unknowns, with $x_{\mathrm p}$ in the first set and $x_{\mathrm f}$ in the second. The matrices $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}$ are formed by relations that hold for every perturbation, such as the continuity of a trace across a side, the symmetry at the plane $z=0$, or the divergence equation on a side. The vectors of unknowns of a cell are complex, and $\langle\mathsf Ax,x\rangle$ denotes the real part of the form of a matrix $\mathsf A$ on a vector $x$.

<!-- source-page: 58 --> A cell has a matrix $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$ on its unknowns and, for each resolved harmonic, two numbers $\underline{\mathsf I}_2>0$ and $\underline{\mathsf I}'_2\geq0$ and a bounded measurable field $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}(r,z)$ of Hermitian $12\times12$ matrices, which act on the pairs $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$. On the cell, $\mathsf I_{2,\iota}\geq\underline{\mathsf I}_2$ and $\mathsf I'_{2,\iota}\geq\underline{\mathsf I}'_2$. The form of $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}(r,z)$ on a pair $(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$ is at most the sum of the other three terms of $\mathcal I_\iota$ minus a form with constant coefficients, which bounds the errors of the polynomial models; and, up to forms whose coefficients are constants or constants divided by $r$, it is at least $\mathcal L(\mathbf G,\mathbf v)$. For every $x=\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}x_{\mathrm g}$, the cell matrix $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$ must satisfy the following comparison. Its forms use the [cell blocks](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Breakdown/CertCell/StatementDefs.lean#L4532-L4578) and the [assembly and pressure conditions](https://github.com/tristanbuckmaster/navier-stokes/blob/ad53419de079eb8f95f60313473374624a348546/lean/Breakdown/CertCell/StatementDefs.lean#L5853-L5897) of the full specification. $$\begin{equation}

 \langle(\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}-\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q})\,x,x\rangle\leq\langle(\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}+\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}-\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q})\,x,x\rangle+\mathsf b_{\mathsf Q}(x)+\mathsf e_{\mathsf Q}(x).
 \tag{B.26}
\end{equation}$$ In (B.26), $\mathsf E_{\mathsf Q}$ uses $\underline{\mathsf I}_2$, $\underline{\mathsf I}'_2$ and the cell-polynomial integrals of $A^{\mathsf Q,\iota}$. The models of $\mathbb S$ and $\mathbb V$ bound $\mathsf P_{\mathsf Q}$ above by the resolved contribution of $J$ less the terms assigned to unresolved harmonics. The resolved-gradient pairings with harmonics of $\nabla b_i$ and $\Xi_i$, weighted by $\beta_i$ and $2\zeta_i$ respectively, bound $\mathsf B_{\mathsf Q}$ above. The form $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ uses the highest-degree gradient coefficients. The eliminated harmonics, which have no unknowns, give $\mathsf b_{\mathsf Q}$. Pairing the right-hand side with the fields of the triples $\varphi$ gives $\mathsf e_{\mathsf Q}$. The component of a resolved mode that is orthogonal to the polynomials of degree at most $\mathsf d$ is controlled by $\underline{\mathsf I}_2$: the terms that it has to absorb are at most $$\begin{equation}
 \underline{\mathsf I}_2\Bigl[r_1\min\bigl(\Lambda^r_{\mathsf d+1},\Lambda^z_{\mathsf d+1}\bigr)+\frac{(|k_{\mathrm{rot}}\,\iota_1|-2)_+^2}{r_2}\Bigr],
 \tag{B.27}
\end{equation}$$ with 1 in place of the factor $r_1$ if $r_1=0$. Here $\Lambda_j^r=j(j+1)\,(2/(r_2-r_1))^2$, or $j(j+2)\,(2/r_2)^2$ on a cell that meets the axis, and $\Lambda_j^z=j(j+1)\,(2/(z_2-z_1))^2$ are the eigenvalues of the Legendre and of the Jacobi $(0,1)$ operators on the intervals of the cell \[[77](#cite-ref77), Tables 18.3.1 and 18.8.1\]. In the radial interval touching the axis, $x=2r/r_2-1$ makes $r\,dr$ a constant multiple of $(1+x)\,dx$, the Jacobi weight with parameters $(0,1)$. The eigenvalues are therefore $j(j+2)$ before rescaling; the Legendre values are $j(j+1)$. The factor from an interval of length $L$ is $(2/L)^2$ \[[77](#cite-ref77), Table 18.3.1, Jacobi and Legendre rows; Table 18.8.1, rows 1 and 7\]. For each harmonic that it does not resolve, a cell has a constant $\mathsf c^*\geq\sqrt{7/2}$ and three bounded measurable functions $\mathsf a'_1$, $\mathsf a_1$ and $\mathsf a_0$ of $(r,z)$; the complement of the cells has one such constant and three such functions for all harmonics, and there the three functions are nonnegative. In a cell that does not resolve $\iota$, and on the complement of the cells, we let $$\begin{equation}
 \mathcal I_\iota^\circ=\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L^\circ(\nabla\hat v_\iota,\hat v_\iota)-\mathsf a'_1\,|\operatorname{curl}\hat v_\iota|^2-\mathsf a_1\,|\nabla\hat v_\iota|^2-\mathsf a_0\,|\hat v_\iota|^2,
 \tag{B.28}
\end{equation}$$ where $\mathcal L^\circ$ is (B.25) with $\mathsf c^*$ in place of $\sqrt{7/2}$.

Near the plane $y_3=0$ there may be finitely many rectangles $\Pi=[r_1,r_2]\times[0,z_2]$ with $r_1>0$ in the union of the cells. Each rectangle has a harmonic $\iota$ resolved in the cells along a segment of $z=0$; neither $\iota^\flat$ nor $-\iota^\flat$ is resolved or eliminated in any cell. Its matrix $\mathsf C_\Pi$ acts on moments, along these plane segments, of the $\mathbf e_z$ component of $\hat v_\iota$. The vector $\mathsf X_\Pi x_{\mathrm g}$ selects these moments from the cell vectors $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}x_{\mathrm g}$. The conditions on a rectangle are a bound, by a positive definite matrix, for a weighted Dirichlet integral over $\Pi$ of the combinations of finitely many given functions, which vanish on the three other sides of $\Pi$ and whose traces on the plane, multiplied by $r$, are combinations of the polynomials of the moments, and a comparison of $\mathsf C_\Pi$ with the inverse of this matrix.

A harmonic that is not resolved in a cell, and every harmonic on the complement of the cells, is subject to a condition on scalars at every point, which bears on the form (B.28). For each cell and each harmonic that is not resolved in it, and for each harmonic on the complement of the cells, we are given finitely many regions of the quarter plane, each with a set of harmonics, possibly infinite, which contains the harmonic for which the region is given, with a number $k_0$ such that $|k_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1|\geq k_0$ on this set, with lower bounds $\underline{\mathsf I}_2$, $\underline{\mathsf I}'_2$, $\underline{\mathsf I}'_1$, $\underline{\mathsf I}_1$ and $\underline{\mathsf I}_0$ for the five coefficients of $\mathcal I_\iota$ which hold on the region for all the harmonics of the set, and with a function $\mathsf t\geq0$ or, if the region reaches infinity, with the four numbers of (B.30). The regions of a cell and a <!-- source-page: 59 --> harmonic cover the cell; those of a harmonic on the complement lie in the complement, cover it and overlap only in sets of measure zero. On a region, with the constant $\mathsf c^*$ and the three functions of the cell and the harmonic for which it is given, or of the complement, let $$
 \mathsf f_2=\underline{\mathsf I}_2,\quad
 \mathsf f'_2=\underline{\mathsf I}'_2,\quad
 \mathsf f'_1=\underline{\mathsf I}'_1-\mathsf s_1-\mathsf a'_1,\quad
 \mathsf f_1=\underline{\mathsf I}_1-\tfrac12\mathsf c^*\mathsf s_3\,\mathsf h-\mathsf a_1,\quad
 \mathsf f_0=\underline{\mathsf I}_0-\frac{\mathsf c^*\mathsf s_3}{2\,\mathsf h}-\mathsf a_0,\quad
 \mathsf f_{01}=\mathsf c^*\mathsf s_2,
$$ and $$
 \mathsf f_1^*=\mathsf f_1+2\min\bigl(\mathsf f'_1+\mathsf f'_2\,(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2,\,0\bigr)+\mathsf f_2\,(k_0-2)_+^2/r^2,\qquad
 \mathsf f_0^*=\mathsf f_0+\mathsf t\,(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2.
$$ The condition is that, at every point of the region, $$\begin{equation}
 \mathsf f_2\geq0,\qquad0\leq\mathsf t\leq\mathsf f_1^*,\qquad\mathsf f_0^*\geq0,\qquad\mathsf f_{01}^2\leq4\,(\mathsf f_1^*-\mathsf t)\,\mathsf f_0^*.
 \tag{B.29}
\end{equation}$$ Some of the regions on the complement of the cells reach infinity: they are sets on which $|(r,z)|$ exceeds a radius, which may depend on the direction, or, for harmonics with $\iota_1=0$, sets $\{r>a\text{ or }z>a\}$ with a given number $a>0$. On these the condition is not pointwise. We require $\mathsf f_2\geq0$, $\mathsf f_1^*\geq\mathsf f_1^\infty$, $|(r,z)|^2\max(-\mathsf f_0,0)\leq\mathsf f_0^\infty$ and $|(r,z)|\,\mathsf f_{01}\leq\mathsf f_{01}^\infty$, with numbers such that $$\begin{equation}
 \frac{\mathsf f_0^\infty}{\Lambda_0}+\frac{\mathsf f_{01}^\infty}{\sqrt{\Lambda_0}}\leq\mathsf f_1^\infty,\qquad
 0<\Lambda_0\leq\tfrac14+(k_0-1)_+^2\quad\text{or}\quad0<\Lambda_0\leq2\quad\text{respectively},
 \tag{B.30}
\end{equation}$$ and the form is integrated over the region $Z$, with the inequality $$\begin{equation}
 \Lambda_0\int_Z\frac{|\hat v_\iota|^2}{|(r,z)|^2}\,r\,dr\,dz\leq\int_Z|\nabla\hat v_\iota|^2\,r\,dr\,dz.
 \tag{B.31}
\end{equation}$$

*One interior cell.* On an interior cell $\mathsf Q=[r_1,r_2]\times[z_1,z_2]$ with $r_1,z_1>0$, write a resolved mode as $E_\iota(u_r,u_\phi,u_z)$ in the cylindrical frame. Its divergence equation is $\partial_r(ru_r)+i k_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1u_\phi+r\partial_z u_z=0$. For the constant test polynomial, put $k=k_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1$ and integrate over $\mathsf Q$. The resulting moment relation is $$
\int_{z_1}^{z_2}[r u_r]_{r_1}^{r_2}\,dz
 +\int_{r_1}^{r_2}r[u_z]_{z_1}^{z_2}\,dr
 +ik\int_{\mathsf Q}u_\phi\,dr\,dz=0.
$$ Thus one volume moment and four side fluxes obey a linear relation. On a common radial side the two outward fluxes have opposite signs. The map $\mathsf X_{\mathsf Q}x_{\mathrm g}$ reads a shared trace from the same coordinates on either side. For the axial component of a momentum test, let $p_\iota$ denote the pressure coefficient and $\psi(r,z)$ the axial test polynomial. Integration by parts gives $$
 \int_{\mathsf Q}r\,\partial_z p_\iota\,\overline\psi
 =\int_{r_1}^{r_2}r[p_\iota\overline\psi]_{z_1}^{z_2}\,dr
   -\int_{\mathsf Q}r\,p_\iota\,\partial_z\overline\psi ,
$$ where the cell integrals use $dr\,dz$. This exhibits the pressure trace in a momentum row. For a spatially constant pressure shift the two terms it adds on the right cancel by the fundamental theorem of calculus. The assembled form must respect the pressure freedoms specified in (B.26).

For example, if a scalar entry $a$ of a coefficient is represented by $a_{\rm mod}$ with $|a-a_{\rm mod}|\le\epsilon$ on $\mathsf Q$, the omitted cross term on two polynomial components $P_1,P_2$ has magnitude at most $2\epsilon\int_{\mathsf Q}|P_1P_2|\,r\,dr\,dz\le\epsilon\int_{\mathsf Q}(|P_1|^2+|P_2|^2)\,r\,dr\,dz$. The constant-coefficient error form preceding (B.26) reserves this amount from the lower bound. The modeled contribution is a matrix entry obtained by integrating the two basis polynomials against $a_{\rm mod}\,r\,dr\,dz$. The first omitted degree in (B.27) contributes the smaller of the two rescaled Legendre eigenvalues times $r_1\underline{\mathsf I}_2$. Angular differentiation bounds the eliminated modes; (B.28)–(B.31) cover the other unrepresented ones. Thus (B.33) bounds the actual mode, including its polynomial remainder. Proposition B.8 sums the cell inequalities using (B.34) for their shared terms and (B.32) on the exterior.

changes.adapted_text: The linear estimate (7.33) requires bounds on several fields paired with the perturbation. Throughout the rest of this subsection, $\iint$ means integration over $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$ with measure $dy\,d\theta$. We say that a measurable field $\mathsf R$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ of period $1$ in $\theta$ has the *dual bound* $\mathsf n$ if $\mathsf R=\mathsf R'+\mathsf R''$ <!-- source-page: 66 --> and there are numbers $\mathsf n',\mathsf n''\ge0$ with $\mathsf n'+\mathsf n''\le\mathsf n$ such that $2\,\||y|\,\mathsf R'\|_{\mathcal H}\le\mathsf n'$ and $\mathsf R''$ is of the following kind: each of the components $\mathsf R''_1+i\,\mathsf R''_2$, $\mathsf R''_1-i\,\mathsf R''_2$ and $\mathsf R''_3$ is a finite sum of terms $e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$, where $k'$ is an integer and $g$ is a measurable function with an azimuthal wave number $k$, that is, $g(R_{\phi_0}y)=e^{ik\phi_0}g(y)$ for every angle $\phi_0$, with distinct pairs $(k',k)$ in each component, and the sum of the numbers $(|k|+\tfrac12)^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|y|^2\,|g|^2\,dy$ over all the terms, those of the first two components counted with the factor $\tfrac12$, is at most $\mathsf n''^2$.

*Proof.* Let $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. Since $f_*$ vanishes for $|y|\le r_\chi$, the radial phase $f_\alpha(|y|^2)$ coincides in $B_{r_\chi}$ with $f(|y|^2)$, with all its derivatives. The fields $W_\alpha^i$ and the functions $q^i$ depend on the phase only through the factors $E_{\iota,l}$ and the operators $\mathcal V_l$ of (B.5); hence in $\mathbb R\times B_{r_\chi}$ they coincide, with their derivatives, with $W_0^i$ and with the functions $q^i$ for the phase $f$. In the formula for $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ of Subsection B.1 we substitute $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=W_0^0+\sum_i\alpha_iW_0^i$, $q_\alpha=q^0+\sum_i\alpha_iq^i$, $1/S(\alpha)=1/S(0)+\varsigma\cdot\alpha$ and $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)=\beta^0+\sum_i\alpha_i\beta^i$, and we collect the powers of $\alpha$: almost everywhere in $\mathbb R\times B_{r_\chi}$, $$
F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}=F^{(0)}+\sum_i\alpha_i\,F^{(i)}+\sum_{i\le i'}\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}\,F^{(ii')}.
$$ The fields (B.57) are bounded on $(0,1)\times B_{r_\chi}$ (Subsection B.1), and $$
\begin{aligned}
V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_j\rangle_{\mathcal H}-d_j\,\alpha_j={}&\bigl[V_j\cdot\beta^0-\langle F^{(0)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi\bigr]+\sum_i\alpha_i\bigl[V_j\cdot\beta^i-\langle F^{(i)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi\bigr]-d_j\,\alpha_j\\
&-\sum_{i\le i'}\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}\,\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi-\bigl\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi},\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\bigr\rangle_{\mathcal H}.
\end{aligned}
$$ By (B.58) the first bracket is at most $|\mathsf C_j^0|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_j^0$ in absolute value, the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ is at most $|\mathsf C_{ji}^1|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{ji}^1$ for $i\ne j$ and, with the term $-d_j\,\alpha_j$, at most $|\mathsf C_{jj}^1-d_j|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{jj}^1$ for $i=j$, and the coefficient of $\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}$ is at most $|\mathsf C_{jii'}^2|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{jii'}^2$. $$ By (B.58) the first bracket is at most $|\mathsf C_j^0|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_j^0$ in absolute value, the coefficient of $\alpha_i$ is at most $|\mathsf C_{ji}^1|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{ji}^1$ for $i\ne j$ and, with the term $-d_j\,\alpha_j$, at most $|\mathsf C_{jj}^1-d_j|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{jj}^1$ for $i=j$, and the coefficient of $\alpha_i\,\alpha_{i'}$ is at most $|\mathsf C_{jii'}^2|+\tilde{\mathsf C}_{jii'}^2$. The last term is at most $\mathsf n_F^{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathsf n_j^{\mathrm{out}}$. Finally $|\alpha_i|\le\hat\varrho_i$, by (7.29): for $i\notin\mathcal J$ because $d_i^2\alpha_i^2\le\varrho_*^2$. Hence the left-hand side is at most the number $o_j$ of (B.59) in absolute value. Since $\bar\ell\equiv0$, this is (7.34). $\square$

The conditions that we have not written out are of the same kinds as those above. Besides the expressions of the coefficients of (B.16) and lower bounds for them, they concern the normalization of the pressure in the cells, under which the matrix of a cell is invariant when a constant is added to its pressure; the rules by which the unknowns of the cells are expressed through the global ones; the parts of $W^{\mathrm r}$ and of its derivatives that the polynomial models leave out, and the groups of harmonics that they couple; the bounds for the errors that are absorbed in each cell; the rectangles near the plane $y_3=0$; and the symmetry of these data under $\iota\mapsto-\iota$. In this appendix we describe how the field from which the approximate profiles of the certificate of Subsection 1.1 are formed was found, and how further fields of this certificate were computed from it, and we show this field (Figures 1 to 4).

We write $\bar W$ for the computed approximate profile, as a field of the self-similar variables $(s,y)$, and $\bar S$ for its period in $s$. In the variable $\theta=s/\bar S$ it is a field of the form (B.6) of Subsection B.1, and the approximate profiles of the certificate are formed from it: in a ball about the origin they are the affine combinations of $\bar W$ with the fields of Subsection C.4, as in (B.9).

changes.adapted_text:
The continuation in Subsection C.3 leads to the angular wave number $k_{\mathrm{rot}}=19$. This is the rotational order used in (B.1) for the reported example. The construction does not establish a least admissible order. The harmonics (B.2) and the coefficient relations of Subsection B.1 make $\bar W$ invariant under rotation by $2\pi/19$ about the $y_3$ axis and under $R_*$, the rotation by $\pi$ about the $y_1$ axis. Advancing $s$ by half a period rotates the field by $\pi/19$: $$
\bar W\bigl(s+\tfrac12\bar S,y\bigr)=R_{\pi/19}\,\bar W\bigl(s,R_{\pi/19}^{-1}\,y\bigr)\qquad(s\in\mathbb R,\ y\in\mathbb R^3).
$$ For $\iota_2=0$, the harmonic $E_\iota$ depends on $\theta$ and $\phi$ through $\phi-2\pi\theta/19$; for $\iota_1=\iota_2$, it depends on them through $\phi+2\pi\theta/19$. These two families give patterns turning in opposite senses, each through $2\pi/19$ per period, and $R_*$ exchanges them. <!-- source-page: 71 --> Every other harmonic is a product of one harmonic from each family. Indeed, $\iota=(\iota_1-\iota_2,0)+(\iota_2,\iota_2)$, and the phases in (B.2) add. The computed period is $\bar S\approx0.36$.

\bar W\bigl(s+\tfrac12\bar S,y\bigr)=R_{\pi/19}\,\bar W\bigl(s,R_{\pi/19}^{-1}\,y\bigr)\qquad(s\in\mathbb R,\ y\in\mathbb R^3).

and every other harmonic is the product of a harmonic of the first pattern and of one of the second. The computed period is $\bar S\approx0.36$.

Figures 1, 2 and 3 show $\bar W$ at $s=0$. Its vorticity is concentrated in a column about the $y_3$ axis and, on either side of the plane $y_3=0$, in a layer that leaves the column and is divided into nineteen spiral arms (Figure 1). The mean of $\bar W$ over the angle $\phi$ is an axisymmetric field with swirl. Its azimuthal component has opposite signs on the two sides of the plane $y_3=0$, as the invariance under $R_*$ requires. Its azimuthal vorticity is concentrated in a thin layer, which runs along the plane at a distance from it and then turns into the direction of the axis, where it encloses the column, and the level lines of its stream function follow this layer (Figure 2, left and middle). The part of $\bar W$ that depends on $\phi$ is of the same order of magnitude as the mean. Its first harmonics, $e^{\pm19i\phi}$, are largest near the plane, about the outer end of the layer (Figure 2, right), and in a horizontal plane through the layer the vertical component of the vorticity forms nineteen spiral arms, which end in nineteen vortices (Figure 3). The mean over $\phi$ has period $\bar S/2$ in $s$, by the symmetry.
