changes.adapted_text: We impose (C.1) weakly, integrating over one period and $\mathbb R^3$ against fields on the same partition, of the same form with $h=3$ in place of $h=1$. There are as many test fields as unknown coefficients. The test fields are divergence-free, so the pressure term drops out. We evaluate products in $\operatorname{curl}W\times W$ on a grid in the two harmonic angles and use Gauss quadrature on each rectangle. When the period is unknown, its derivative adds a column to the Newton system and a phase condition fixing translation in $s$ adds a row. To judge the current iterate, we evaluate the left-hand side of (C.1) without $\nabla H$ on a larger set of harmonics, subtract a gradient fitted by least squares, and measure the remainder in $\mathcal H$ of Subsection 7.1. For this iterate the measured norm approximates the minimum obtained by varying the pressure coefficients. For the represented family, (7.23) requires bounds on the specified $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ over the whole parameter set, including its pairings in (7.17).

changes.authors_text: The equation is imposed in a weak form. We integrate (C.1) over a period and over $\mathbb R^3$ against fields of the same form on the same partition, with the exponent $h=3$ in place of $h=1$. These test fields are divergence-free, so that the term $\nabla H$ drops out, and there are as many of them as there are unknown coefficients. The products of harmonics in $\operatorname{curl}W\times W$ are formed on a grid in the two angles on which the harmonics depend, the integrals over each rectangle are computed by Gauss quadrature, and one further equation fixes the translation of the field in $s$; it is the equation that belongs to the unknown period. This number approximates the norm in $\mathcal H$ of the left-hand side of (C.1) for the best choice of $H$, and it steers the computation. changes.note: Separates the continuation that reaches g=1/2 from its subsequent reflection and refinement to rotational order nineteen.
changes.adapted_text:
The starting field for Newton’s method is obtained by continuation, first with finite differences and <!-- source-page: 74 --> then with spectral elements. These discretizations precede that of Subsection C.2. The continuation uses the family $$
\partial_sU+(1-g)\,U+g\,(y\cdot\nabla)U+(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla\pi=\nu\,\Delta U+F,\qquad\operatorname{div}U=0,
$$ with scaling parameter $g$, viscosity $\nu>0$ and force $F$. The target is $g=\tfrac12$, $\nu=1$, $F=0$.

*One rotating pattern.* We begin with an axisymmetric steady state at $g$ near $0.502$ and with a small force. It is computed from a field with swirl changing sign across $y_3=0$, an inward-flowing layer along that plane, a column, and an axial jet. On the layer we superpose finite-amplitude waves of azimuthal wave numbers $14$ to $20$, turning rigidly about the axis. We reduce the force to zero along with the damping introduced at this step. We then work in $y_3>0$ with one wave family and allow its azimuthal wave number to be real. Among the unforced families found by continuation, the first stays in $g>\tfrac12$ and a second reaches $g=\tfrac12$. At that value we have an unforced state with the desired scaling.

*Two counter-rotating patterns.* We superpose this state with its oppositely turning image under $R_*$ and impose the exact condition at $y_3=0$. Further refinements use viscosity in place of $g$ as an unknown and bring the wave number to $19$. We finally project the result onto a space of the form used in Subsection C.2.
changes.authors_text:
Newton’s method starts from a field that was reached by continuation, in other discretizations than that of Subsection C.2: finite differences, and <!-- source-page: 74 --> then spectral elements. The continuation takes place in the family of equations $$
\partial_sU+(1-g)\,U+g\,(y\cdot
abla)U+(U\cdot
abla)U+
abla\pi=
u\,\Delta U+F,\qquad\operatorname{div}U=0,
$$ with a scaling parameter $g$, a viscosity $
u>0$ and a force $F$; the first two equations of (1.2) are the case $g=	frac12$, $
u=1$, $F=0$. It begins with an axisymmetric steady state for $g$ near $0.502$ and a small force, computed from a field whose swirl changes sign across the plane $y_3=0$ and which is composed of a layer of fluid that flows inward along the plane, a column, and a jet along the axis. On this layer we superpose waves of finite amplitude, with azimuthal wave numbers from $14$ to $20$, whose dependence on time is a rigid rotation about the axis, and we bring the force to zero, together with a damping term that this step introduces. We then pass to the half space $y_3>0$, with one family of waves and with the azimuthal wave number as a real parameter. Without force the states so computed form two-parameter families, on which $g$ is a function of the parameters; on the first of these $g>	frac12$ everywhere, and the value $g=	frac12$ is reached on a second one. At $g=	frac12$ we superpose such a state and its image under $R_*$, which turns in the opposite sense, and we replace the condition at the plane $y_3=0$ by the exact one. Finally, through several refinements of the discretization, in which the viscosity takes the place of $g$ as an unknown, the wave number is brought to the integer $19$, and the result is projected onto a space of the form of Subsection C.2.

changes.note: Identifies the discretizations at which the viscosity, then the period, are fixed in the computation.
changes.adapted_text:
*Fixing viscosity and period.* Starting from this field, we use nine successive discretizations of Subsection C.2, transferring each computed field to the next set of degrees. In the first three, viscosity and period are unknown, and we normalize the mean swirl. For the continuum equations, solutions at different viscosities are dilations of one another; the normalization chooses one. For $g=	frac12$ and $F=0$, the dilation is $U_
u(s,y)=\sqrt
u\,U_1(s,y/\sqrt
u)$, with $\pi_
u(s,y)=
u\pi_1(s,y/\sqrt
u)$ in the continuation equation. We bring the viscosity to one along this family. The fourth discretization fixes it at one and solves for the period. That period is $ ar S$ and is fixed in the last five discretizations. The ninth field is $ ar W$.
changes.authors_text: From this starting field the approximate profile is computed in nine successive discretizations of the form of Subsection C.2, each of which starts from the field of the one before, transferred to the new degrees. In the first three the viscosity is an unknown beside the period, and a normalization of the mean swirl is imposed: for the equations themselves, the solutions for different viscosities are dilations of one another, and the normalization selects one of them. The viscosity is then brought to one along this family. In the fourth discretization the viscosity is one and the period is an unknown; the period found there is $\bar S$, and it is kept in the five discretizations that follow. The ninth field is $\bar W$.

changes.note: Distinguishes the two degree-selection rules and then states the common far-field rule.
changes.adapted_text: Between discretizations we choose degrees separately for each harmonic and rectangle. One rule raises or lowers them using residual size and coefficient decay, adding omitted harmonics wherever they contribute to the residual. The other uses coefficient decay weighted by the estimated local rates of the equation’s terms. Far out, the radial phase removes the spiral oscillation. The remaining frequencies in $\log|y|$ set the radial degrees, and all rings use the same degrees in $\eta$.
changes.authors_text: Between two discretizations the degrees are changed harmonic by harmonic and rectangle by rectangle, by one of two rules. In the first, the contribution of each harmonic on each rectangle to the residual, and the rate at which its coefficients decay with the degree, decide whether its degrees are raised or lowered, and harmonics are added on the rectangles on which the residual lies outside those that are present. In the second, the degrees are predicted from the decay of the coefficients alone, each weighted by estimates of the local rates of the terms of the equation. Far from the origin, where the radial phase has removed the oscillation of the spiral arms, the degrees in the radius are tied to the frequencies in $\log|y|$ that remain, and the degrees in $\eta$ are the same in all rings.

authors: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#1

sources.where: Sections B.1, B.4 and C.4, in particular (B.53) and (7.35). The original paper, p. 75, describes the two intermediate fields after solenoidal cutoff and smoothing.

changes.note: Distinguishes the computed response directions from the phase pair and traces the rounded gradient defect to the bound used in force cancellation.
adapted: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#1
changes.adapted_text:
We compute $b_i$ and the constraint fields $\Xi_i$ in (7.11) from the equation linearized about one field in the sequence of Subsection C.3. Perturbations are discretized more coarsely than that field. For a given right-hand side, we solve with (C.2), bordered by the period derivative and a condition removing translation in $s$. We measure perturbations in a norm of the form (7.14) with constant weight $w>0$, and right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$. The block Lanczos iteration searches for directions with the largest ratio of solution norm to right-hand-side norm. It returns candidate right-hand sides together with their solutions. We retain finitely many of these pairs. There is one further pair for time translation, whose perturbation is the $s$-derivative of the field. In each pair, the right-hand side gives $b_i$ and the solution $v_i$ gives the constraint <!-- source-page: 75 --> through $w\,v_i-\Delta v_i$. For a divergence-free field $v$, $$
 igl\langle
abla v,
abla(w\,v_i-\Delta v_i) igrangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\Delta v,\Delta v_iangle_{\mathcal H}+w\,\langle
abla v,
abla v_iangle_{\mathcal H}
$$ is the inner product of $v$ and $v_i$ in this norm. For the right-hand side defining $b_i$ and the constraint vector $w\,v_i-\Delta v_i$, we choose the radial cutoff and smoothing so that both fields remain divergence-free and retain their symmetries. For $\Phi_i$ and $\Xi_i$ of Subsection B.1 we repeatedly quarter a meridional cell. Up to normalization, $\Phi_i$ is $r$ times a least-squares spline with coefficients in integer multiples of a power of $2$. The rounded cellwise polynomial $\Xi_i$ approximates $
abla\Phi_i$. The bound $c_\Xi$ controls $\|\sum_i x_i(\Xi_i-
abla\Phi_i)\|_{\mathcal H}$ for every unit vector $x\in\mathbb R^n$. Its contribution $\mathsf n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$ to (B.53) enters $a_j$ in the parameter bound (7.35).
replaced: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#1
changes.authors_text:
The forcing fields $b_i$ and the fields $\Xi_i$ of the constraints (7.11) are computed from the equation linearized about a field of the sequence of Subsection C.3. On a space of perturbations coarser than that of the field, we solve the equation with the operator (C.2) for a given right-hand side, bordered as in Newton’s method by the derivative with respect to the period and by a condition that removes the translation in $s$. Perturbations are measured in a norm of the form of (7.14) with a constant weight $w>0$, and right-hand sides in $\mathcal H$. A block Lanczos iteration gives the right-hand sides for which the solution is largest relative to the right-hand side, with their solutions. Finitely many of these pairs are kept, and to them is added the pair that accounts for the translations in time: the left null vector of the bordered system and the derivative of the field in $s$. For each pair, the forcing field $b_i$ is obtained from the right-hand side, and the constraint from the solution $v_i$, <!-- source-page: 75 --> through the field $w\,v_i-\Delta v_i$: for a divergence-free field $v$, $$
 igl\langle
abla v,
abla(w\,v_i-\Delta v_i) igrangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\Delta v,\Delta v_iangle_{\mathcal H}+w\,\langle
abla v,
abla v_iangle_{\mathcal H}
$$ is the inner product of $v$ and $v_i$ that belongs to this norm. Both fields are cut off in the radius and smoothed, in such a way that they remain divergence-free and keep the symmetries. The fields $\Phi_i$ and $\Xi_i$ of Subsection B.1 are then produced on a mesh of cells of the meridian plane, obtained by repeated division of a cell into four: $\Phi_i$ is, up to a normalization, $r$ times a spline fitted by least squares, whose coefficients are integer multiples of a power of $2$, and $\Xi_i$ is a polynomial on each cell, with rounded coefficients, which approximates $
abla\Phi_i$. This is why $\Xi_i$ is not a gradient, and why Subsection B.1 has the number $c_\Xi$.

changes.note: Applies the similarity transport operator to a scalar oscillatory tail, deriving the coefficient 4π/S and connecting the graph-domain example to physical phase and the parameter-dependent radial phase.
adapted: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#3
changes.adapted_text:
The fields $W^i$ in (B.9), $1\le i\le n$, together with $\beta^i$ and $\varsigma_i$, approximately solve the linearized equation with prescribed constraint values. The unknowns include the coefficients of a force and a change of period. The equation for the first-order residual is $F^{(i)}\simeq0$, with $F^{(i)}$ as in (B.57). Here $\simeq$ means equality modulo gradients as defined in (7.2); the numerical approximation concerns satisfaction of that equation. The logarithmic tail in Subsection 7.1 explains why the radial phase must vary with the period. For $\rho=|y|$ and a nonzero integer $l$, the leading scalar mode $h=\rho^{-1}\exp(il[c\log\rho-2\pi\theta])$ obeys $$
 (S^{-1}\partial_\theta+\tfrac12\rho\partial_\rho+\tfrac12)h
 =il(c/2-2\pi/S)h.
$$ The coefficient $c=4\pi/S$ cancels this term. Leaving $c$ fixed while changing $S$ would leave a term of size $\rho^{-1}$ in this model, outside spatial $L^2$ at infinity. It is the same cancellation that fixes the phase at a physical point in Subsection C.1. Formula (B.9) varies the radial phase by a multiple of $f_*$, which vanishes on $B_{r_\chi}$ and grows logarithmically at infinity. Thus the family stays affine inside the ball, where Lemma B.13 expands the residual to second order. Outside the ball the same lemma uses the separate exterior norm bounds. The adjoint fields $\psi_j$ approximately solve the adjoint linearized equation. As in (7.33), the right-hand sides are combinations of the fields representing the constraints. For each adjoint field $\psi_j$, the vector of its pairings with the forcing fields $b_i$ is prescribed and compared with the column $V_j$ in (7.35). We seek $\psi_j$ with $h=3$.
replaced: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#2
changes.authors_text: The fields $W^i$ of (B.9), $1\le i\le n$, with the vectors $\beta^i$ and the numbers $\varsigma_i$ of Subsection B.1, are computed approximate solutions of the linearized equation in which a combination of the forcing fields and a change of the period are unknowns and the values of the constraints are prescribed: with the field $F^{(i)}$ of (B.57), they solve approximately the equation $F^{(i)}\simeq0$. A change of the period changes the radial phase, which is tied to the period. In these fields the change is made only outside a ball, which is the origin of the function $f_*$ of (B.9), so that inside the ball the approximate profiles are affine in the parameter. The adjoint fields $\psi_j$ are computed approximate solutions of the adjoint of the linearized equation whose right-hand sides are combinations of the fields that represent the constraints, as (7.33) requires, with prescribed pairings with the forcing fields, which (7.35) compares with the columns of the matrix $V$; they are sought with the exponent $h=3$.

sources.where: Subsection B.2, (B.15), and Subsection C.4, fixed rotation rates at the computed period.

changes.note: Derives the rotating-frame frequencies at the base period and the shift at a general parameter. Explains the competition between frequency gain and transport error.
adapted: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#4
changes.adapted_text: The multiplier weights $\lambda_p$ and $\mu_p$ in (B.14) act outside $|\iota_2|\le j_*$, $|\iota_2-\iota_1|\le j_*$. We use rotation rates $\nu_p=\pm2\pi/(19\bar S)$, those of the two patterns in Subsection C.1. At period $\bar S$, (B.15) gives $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$ in the first frame and $-4\pi(\iota_1-\iota_2)/\bar S$ in the second. Outside the stated range, at least one then has modulus greater than $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. At period $S(\alpha)$ one must add $2\pi(2\iota_2-\iota_1)(S(\alpha)^{-1}-\bar S^{-1})$ to each expression. Admissibility in Subsection B.2 requires the frequency bounds for every $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. The multiplier supplies positive terms proportional to $\lambda_p|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ and $\mu_p|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ in (B.16). This uses the nonnegative weights and the positive-frequency condition on each $\mathcal N_p$ from Subsection B.2; the sign in (B.14) treats $-\mathcal N_p$. These terms must absorb errors including transport by $W^{\mathrm r}+\tfrac12y-\nu_p\,\mathbf e_z\times y$, the velocity relative to that frame. Considering only this error and omitting weight derivatives, the best pointwise weight is proportional to frequency divided by the square of this speed. For positive fixed auxiliary factors and nonzero speed, this follows by maximizing the linear frequency gain minus the quadratic transport error as a function of the weight. The weights are splines in (B.3). Numerical optimization chooses their coefficients to maximize the least, over cells and harmonic classes, of the suitably normalized differences between the two sides of the inequalities containing them.
replaced: C.4 Further fields of the certificate#3
changes.authors_text: The weights $\lambda_p$ and $\mu_p$ of the multiplier (B.14) act on the harmonics outside the range $|\iota_2|\le j_*$, $|\iota_2-\iota_1|\le j_*$. In the computation the rates of rotation $\nu_p$ are, up to the sign, the angular velocity $2\pi/(19\,\bar S)$ of the two patterns of Subsection C.1. In the frame that turns with the first pattern the frequency (B.15) of the harmonic $\iota$ is $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$, and in the frame that turns with the second it is $-4\pi(\iota_1-\iota_2)/\bar S$: outside the range each harmonic has, in one of the two frames, a frequency of modulus larger than $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. The multiplier turns this frequency into positive terms, proportional to $\lambda_p\,|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ and to $\mu_p\,|\Omega_p(\iota)|$, in the coefficients of (B.16). Among the errors that these terms have to absorb is the transport by $W^{\mathrm r}+\tfrac12y-\nu_p\,\mathbf e_z\times y$, the velocity relative to this frame; if this error alone is taken into account, without the derivatives of the weight, the best weight at a point is proportional to the frequency divided by the square of this speed. The weights are splines in the variables (B.3), and their coefficients are found by a numerical optimization, which maximizes the smallest, over the cells and over the classes of harmonics, of the differences between the two sides of the inequalities in which the weights enter, each suitably normalized.

adapted: Original authors’ statement on AI use#1
changes.adapted_text: We used Anthropic models (Claude) throughout this work, and no others. The work builds on unreleased work of the authors on computer-assisted proofs, in particular concerning the non-uniqueness of Leray–Hopf solutions in the style of Jia and Šverák \[[65](#cite-ref65)\] and blow-up for fluid equations with boundary. It builds also on numerical work of the authors on finding self-similar profiles, on our earlier papers on singularity formation, and on our unreleased drafts on the forced hypodissipative Navier–Stokes equations and the forced Navier–Stokes equations. The idea of pursuing discretely self-similar solutions came from the paper of the second author with Coiculescu and Li on non-uniqueness \[[17](#cite-ref17)\]. The agents were given a curated dossier of potential leads and then guidance after our strictly-uncontaminated experiment producing unforced Euler and forced Navier–Stokes blow-up from our forced Euler and forced hypodissipative Navier–Stokes manuscripts. A simpler mechanism sufficed to produce unforced hyperdissipative Navier–Stokes blow-up, i.e. for $\nu\cdot(-\Delta)^{\frac{501}{500}}$, and then a heavier computation produced this profile. We used the enslopification skills of Scott Armstrong \[[10](#cite-ref10)\] to create a draft from an initial Lean proof (Subsection 1.5); the draft followed that proof step by step. We then rewrote it with Claude under our direction, citing standard results in place of proofs and simplifying the argument over successive revisions, so that the proof given here no longer follows the Lean proof.
